## **Troubleshooting Tips**

If you encounter issues, such as not seeing any metrics being ingested from the Prometheus endpoints, consider the following tips to identify and resolve the problem:

1.   **Inspect the Logs of the OpenTelemetry Collector Pods**: The logs of the collector pods can provide valuable insights when you don't see any metrics coming in from the Prometheus endpoints. These logs may contain debugging information that can help pinpoint any issues with the scraping of the endpoints.You can check the logs of the collector pods by using the kubectl logs command. Suppose your OpenTelemetry Collector pod is named otel-collector-abcde, you can view its logs with the following command:

```markup
kubectl logs otel-collector-abcde
```

To continuously stream the logs, add the -f flag as shown below:

```markup
kubectl logs -f otel-collector-abcde
```

Replace app.kubernetes.io/name=otel-collector with the appropriate label selector for your OpenTelemetry Collector pods.

1.   **Understand the Role of the Service Discovery (SD) Config**: To view the SD Config, you need to inspect the configuration of your OpenTelemetry Collector. Depending on how you have deployed the collector, this configuration might be located in a ConfigMap, a command-line argument, or a file in the pod. If it's in a ConfigMap, you can view it with:

```markup
kubectl get configmap otel-collector-config -o yaml
```

If the configuration is passed as a command-line argument or a file, you might need to examine the pod specification or access the pod's filesystem to find it. To inspect the pod specification, use:

```markup
kubectl get pod otel-collector-abcde -o yaml
```

1.   **Datapoints being dropped:**There are certain organizational level dashboards which could help in finding if there are any throttling issues at thecollector/token level which might stop the data points from being ingested into the platform.
2.   Start by looking at the dashboards here.Dashboards ->[Built-in Dashboard Groups](https://us1.signalfx.com/o11y/) ->[Organization metrics](https://us1.signalfx.com/o11y/) -> IMM Throttling
3.   Look at the token throttling and data points dropped dashboards, which will look something like below:

![Image 6: rohits_4-1691443766091.png](https://community.splunk.com/t5/image/serverpage/image-id/26671iD055E541E2EB39BB/image-size/large?v=v2&px=999)rohits_4-1691443766091.png

![Image 7: rohits_5-1691443766159.png](https://community.splunk.com/t5/image/serverpage/image-id/26672iA54987D10ABBBEA2/image-size/large?v=v2&px=999)rohits_5-1691443766159.png

1.   Start by looking at the collector pods which would give you the metrics which are getting dropped. The logs may look like this:

```markup
2023-07-20T22:45:51.977Z debug translation/converter.go:240 dropping datapoint {"kind": "exporter", "data_type": "metrics", "name": "signalfx", "reason": "number of dimensions is larger than 36", "datapoint": "source:\"\" metric:\"controller_invocations_contentLength_total
```

Splunk will drop the data points/MTS if they don't follow certain standards , like in the above case the number of dimensions reached more than **36**.[Read more.](https://docs.splunk.com/Observability/metrics-and-metadata/metrics-dimensions-mts.html#nav-Dimensions-custom-properties-and-tags)

1.   The best way to eliminate throttling and get rid of these errors is to drop these metrics at the prometheus receiver level if they are not required.**metric_relabel_configs**is the important key here. [Read more](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/tree/main/receiver/prometheusreceiver).

```markup
receivers:

prometheus:

   config:

     scrape_configs:

       - job_name: 'otel-collector'

         scrape_interval: 5s

         static_configs:

           - targets: ['0.0.0.0:8888']

       - job_name: k8s

         kubernetes_sd_configs:

         - role: pod

         relabel_configs:

         - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape]

           regex: "true"

           action: keep

         metric_relabel_configs:

         - source_labels: [__name__]

           regex: "(request_duration_seconds.*|response_duration_seconds.*)"

           action: keep
```

1.   Another error that can cause data points to be dropped and token throttling could be this:2023-07-21T17:28:49.553Z debug translation/converter.go:105 Datapoint does not match the filter, skipping {"kind": "exporter", "data_type": "metrics", "name": "signalfx", "dp": "source:\"\" metric:\"k8s.pod.memory.working_set\"

The above error shows that the Signalfx exporter is skipping this metric as it is excluded by default from the exporter.These errors can be ignored as they are expected out of k8s clusters. [Read more](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/tree/main/exporter/signalfxexporter#default-metric-filters).

args.summary:
This Splunk Community blog article (by Splunk employee "rohits", published August 10, 2023) provides a comprehensive step-by-step guide for monitoring Spinnaker infrastructure and services running on Kubernetes (K8s) using Splunk Observability Cloud and the Splunk Platform. Spinnaker is an open-source, multi-cloud continuous delivery platform composed of microservices, each exposing metrics that can be scraped by the Splunk Distribution of the OpenTelemetry collector.

**Key Spinnaker services to monitor** (with recommended metrics): Deck (UI - load times, error rates, user activity), Gate (API gateway - error rates, request/response times, traffic), Orca (orchestration engine - task execution times, failure rates, queue length), Clouddriver (mutating operations & caching - cache times, error rates), Front50 (metadata store - read/write times, data volumes), Rosco (machine images - baking times, queue lengths), Echo (eventing - delivery times, queue lengths), Fiat (authorization - authorization times, volume), and Igor (CI integration - job completion times, queue lengths).

**Article workflow (5 main steps):**
1. **Enable Prometheus endpoints** - Use Armory's Observability plugin (which exposes metrics via Prometheus endpoints), with installation link provided. Connecting to Splunk Observability is done via the OpenTelemetry collector scraping the endpoints.
2. **Install Splunk OpenTelemetry collector** - Deploy using Helm chart on the Spinnaker K8s cluster. Includes sample custom values.yaml snippets for configuring splunkPlatform (endpoint, token, index) and splunkObservability (realm us1, ingestUrl https://ingest.us1.signalfx.com, metricsEnabled: true). Includes a prometheus/spinnaker receiver config using kubernetes_sd_configs with role: pod and metrics_path /aop-prometheus (with insecure_skip_verify: true noted as a security risk). Sample install command: `helm install splunk-otel-collector splunk-otel-collector-chart/splunk-otel-collector -f condensed_values.yaml`.
3. **Verify metrics ingestion** - Curl the /aop-prometheus endpoint (https://localhost:7002/aop-prometheus) to find metric names, enable collector debug logging (telemetry logs level "debug"), and use Splunk SignalFlow queries (e.g., `A = data('*', filter=filter('sf_metric', '*') and filter('k8s.pod.name', 'spin-orca-*')).count(by=['sf_metric']).publish(label='A')`).
4. **Create Spinnaker metrics dashboard** - No out-of-the-box (OOTB) Splunk dashboards exist for Spinnaker. Instead, leverage open-source Grafana dashboards (from uneeq-oss/spinnaker-mixin repository) and translate their queries into SignalFlow expressions. A detailed example converts a Grafana Orca controller_invocations query into SignalFlow (A = sum of controller_invocations_seconds_sum, B = sum of controller_invocations_seconds_count, C = A/B).
5. **Enable Armory Continuous Deployment logging** - Log data about accounts/functions via direct push to Splunk HEC endpoints (Developer Insights), and import available JSON dashboards into Splunk (default index is "spinnaker" - may need modification).

**Troubleshooting tips:**
- Inspect OpenTelemetry collector pod logs (kubectl logs / kubectl logs -f otel-collector-abcde)
- Examine Service Discovery config in ConfigMap (`kubectl get configmap otel-collector-config -o yaml`) or pod spec (`kubectl get pod otel-collector-abcde -o yaml`)
- Check for datapoint throttling via built-in dashboards (Dashboards -> Built-in Dashboard Groups -> Organization metrics -> IMM Throttling; examine token throttling and datapoint dropped dashboards)
- Datapoints get dropped if dimensions exceed 36 (e.g., "reason": "number of dimensions is larger than 36")
- Use metric_relabel_configs to drop unnecessary metrics at the prometheus receiver level
- Some errors (e.g., "Datapoint does not match the filter, skipping" for k8s.pod.memory.working_set) are expected/ignorable due to default signalfx exporter metric filters

The article is tagged with labels Observability and OpenTelemetry, and tags k8s, Microservices, observability, Observability Cloud, and Spinnaker. It concludes by inviting readers to start a free trial of Splunk Observability platform.

# From Spinnaker – Monitoring Spinnaker: SLA Metrics

By [cdfoundation](https://cd.foundation/author/cdfoundation/)March 11, 2020November 1st, 2023[Blog](https://cd.foundation/category/blog/), [Project](https://cd.foundation/category/blog/project/)

[No Comments](https://cd.foundation/blog/2020/03/11/from-spinnaker-monitoring-spinnaker-sla-metrics/#respond)

*Originally posted on the [Spinnaker Community blog](https://blog.spinnaker.io/spinnaker-n8b-diary-1-430b7c1d6832), by Rob Zienert, Sr Software Engineer @ Netflix*

Long, long ago, in an internet that I barely remember, [I wrote about monitoring Orca](https://blog.spinnaker.io/monitoring-spinnaker-part-1-4847f42a3abd). I haven’t managed to take the time to write another post about a specific service — it’s a lot of work! Instead of going deep this time around, I want to paint with broader strokes: What are the key metrics we can track that help quickly answer the question, “Is Spinnaker healthy?”

Spinnaker is comprised of about a dozen open source services that may vary widely based on configuration, and as such, there’s no singular metric to rule them all. This makes the question, “Is Spinnaker healthy?” a particularly bothersome question since not all services are equally important. If Igor — [the service that is responsible for monitoring CI/SCM systems](https://github.com/spinnaker/igor/blob/master/README.md)— is unable to communicate with Jenkins, Spinnaker will be in a degraded state, but its core behavior is still healthy. Should Orca’s queue processing drop to zero, however, it’s time to have an elevated heart rate and quick remedy.

# Service Metrics

The Service Level Indicators for our individual services can vary depending on configuration. For example, Clouddriver has cloud provider-specific metrics that should be tracked in addition to its core metrics. For the sake of this post’s length, I won’t be going into any cloud-specific metrics.

## Universal Metrics

All Spinnaker services are RPC-based, and as such, the reliability of requests inbound and outbound are supremely important: If the services can’t talk to each other reliably, someone will be having a poor experience.

For each service, a `controller.invocations` metric is emitted, which is a `PercentileTimer` including the following tags:

* `status`: The HTTP status code family, `2xx, 3xx, 4xx...`
* `statusCode`: The actual HTTP status code value, `204, 302, 429...`
* `success`: If the request is considered successful. There’s nuance here in the `4xx` range, but `2xx` and`3xx` are definitely all successful, whereas `5xx` definitely are not
* `controller`: The Spring Controller class that served this request
* `method`: The Spring Controller method name, NOT the HTTP method

Similarly, each service also emits metrics for each RPC client that is configured via `okhttp.requests`. That is, Orca will have a variety of metrics for its Echo client, as well as its Clouddriver client. This metric has the following tags:

* `status`: The HTTP status code family, `2xx, 3xx, 4xx...`
* `statusCode`: The actual HTTP status code value, `204, 302, 429...`
* `success`: If the request is considered successful
* `authenticated`: Whether or not the request was authenticated or anonymous (if Fiat is disabled, this is always `false`)
* `requestHost`: The DNS name of the client. Depending on your topology, some services may have more than one client to a particular service (like Igor to Jenkins, or Orca to Clouddriver shards).

![](https://cd.foundation/wp-content/uploads/sites/35/2020/03/1_RLOQXsdcflveany-Y0gQSQ-1024x298.png)

Example of our 24/7 request fanout from Gate. One interesting tidbit: The sudden increase in traffic at 9am is the increased traffic to Clouddriver (bottom) from Chaos Monkey starting its daily light mayhem!

Having SLOs — and consequentially, alerts — around failure rate (determined via the `succcess` tag) and latency for both inbound and outbound RPC requests is, in my mind, mandatory across all Spinnaker services.

As a real world example, the alert Netflix uses for Orca to all of its client services is:

```
nf.cluster,orca-main.*,:re,  
name,okhttp.requests,:eq,:and,  
status,(,Unknown,5xx,),:in,:and,  
statistic,count,:eq,:and,  
:sum,  
(,nf.cluster,),:by,  
0.2,:gt,3,  
:rolling-count,3,:ge
```

So, for people who can’t read [Atlas expressions](https://github.com/Netflix/atlas/wiki/Alerting-Expressions), if we have more than 0.2 failing/unknown RPS to a specific service over 3 minutes, we’ll get an alert.

## Service-specific Metrics

Most of our services have an additional metric to judge operational health, but in/out RPC monitoring will go far if you’re just starting out.

* **Echo**  
  `echo.triggers.count` tracks the number of CRON-triggered pipeline executions fired. This value should be pretty steady, so any significant deviation is an indicator of something going awry (or the addition/retirement of a customer integration).  
  `echo.pubsub.messagesProcessed` is important if you have any PubSub triggers. Your mileage may vary, but Netflix can alert if any subscriptions drop to zero for more than a few minutes.

* **Orca**  
  `task.invocations.duration` tracks how long individual queue tasks take to execute. While it is a Timer, for an SLA Metric, its count is what’s important. This metric’s value can vary widely, but if it drops to zero, it means Orca isn’t processing any new work, so Spinnaker is dead in the water from a core behavior perspective.

* **Clouddriver**: Each cloud provider is going to emit its own metrics that can help determine health, but two universal ones I recommend tracking are related to its cache.  
  `cache.drift` tracks cache freshness. You should group this by `agent` and `region` to be granular on exactly what cache collection is falling behind. How much lag is acceptable for your org is up to you, but don’t make it zero.  
  `executionCount` tracks the number of caching agent executions and combined with `status` , we can track how many specific caching agents are failing at any given time.

![](https://cd.foundation/wp-content/uploads/sites/35/2020/03/1_RCadDVvouj8mpkTJSEfdkQ-1024x298.png)

Here, one collection for a specific AWS service in our largest region was getting stale. In this case, while AWS availability was fine for Clouddriver, Edda was having trouble refreshing.

 ![](https://cd.foundation/wp-content/uploads/sites/35/2020/03/1_XfrOpTWXHeCh5gvPax2l4g-1024x207.png)

It’s OK that there are failures in agents: As stable as we like to think our cloud providers are, it’s still another software system and software will fail. Unless you see sustained failure, there’s not much to worry about here. This is often an indicator of a downstream cloud provider issue.

* **Igor**  
  `pollingMonitor.failed` tracks the failure rate of CI/SCM monitor poll cycles. Any value above 0 is a bad place to be, but is often a result of downstream service availability issues such as Jenkins going offline for maintenance.  
  `pollingMonitor.itemsOverThreshold` tracks a polling monitor circuit breaker. Any value over 0 is a bad time, because it means the breaker is open for a particular monitor and it requires [manual intervention](https://github.com/spinnaker/igor/blob/master/igor-web/src/main/groovy/com/netflix/spinnaker/igor/admin/AdminController.java#L58).

# Product SLAs at Netflix

We also track specific metrics as they pertain to some of our close internal customers. Some customers care most about latency reading our cloud cache, others have strict requirements in latency and reliability of ad-hoc pipeline executions.

In addition to tracking our own internal metrics for each customer, we also subscribe to our customers’ alerts against Spinnaker. If internal metrics don’t alert us of a problem before our customers are aware something is wrong, we at least don’t want to wait for our customers to tell us.

# Continued Observability Improvements

Since Spinnaker is such a large, varied system, blog posts such as these are fine, but really are meant to get the wheels turning on what could be possible. It also highlights a problem with Spinnaker today: A lack of easily discoverable operational insights and knobs. No one should have to rely on a core contributor to distill information like this into a blog post!

There’s already been a start to improving automated service configuration property documentation, but something similar needs to be started for metrics and matching admin APIs as well. A contribution that documents metrics, their tags, purpose and related alerts would be of huge impact to the project and something I’d be happy to mentor on and/or jumpstart.

Of course, if you want to get involved in improving Spinnaker’s operational characteristics, there’s [a Special Interest Group](https://github.com/spinnaker/governance/tree/master/sig-ops) for that. We’d love to see you there!

args.key_excerpts: Having SLOs — and consequentially, alerts — around failure rate (determined via the success tag) and latency for both inbound and outbound RPC requests is, in my mind, mandatory across all Spinnaker services., No one should have to rely on a core contributor to distill information like this into a blog post!, A contribution that documents metrics, their tags, purpose and related alerts would be of huge impact to the project and something I'd be happy to mentor on and/or jumpstart.
args.summary:
This blog post, originally published on the Spinnaker Community blog by Rob Zienert (Sr Software Engineer @ Netflix) and reposted by the CD Foundation (March 11, 2020), provides guidance on monitoring Spinnaker's health through Service Level Agreement (SLA) metrics. The author addresses the core question "Is Spinnaker healthy?" noting that Spinnaker comprises about a dozen open source services whose importance varies—for example, if Igor (the CI/SCM monitoring service) can't communicate with Jenkins, Spinnaker is degraded but still functional, whereas Orca's queue processing dropping to zero represents a critical emergency.

KEY POINTS:

1. UNIVERAL METRICS: Since all Spinnaker services are RPC-based, request reliability is paramount. Each service emits:
   - `controller.invocations` - A PercentileTimer with tags including status (HTTP status family like 2xx, 3xx, 4xx), statusCode (actual code), success (requests considered successful), controller (Spring Controller class), and method (Spring Controller method name, not HTTP method).
   - `okhttp.requests` - Metrics for each configured RPC client, with tags including status, statusCode, success, authenticated (whether Fiat was used), and requestHost (client DNS name, relevant for multi-client topologies like Igor to Jenkins or Orca to Clouddriver shards).

2. NETFLIX EXAMPLE ALERT: Netflix uses an Atlas expression alert for Orca that triggers if there are more than 0.2 failing/unknown RPS to a specific service over 3 minutes.

3. SERVICE-SPECIFIC METRICS:
   - Echo: `echo.triggers.count` tracks CRON-triggered pipeline executions (should be steady); `echo.pubsub.messagesProcessed` monitors PubSub triggers (Netflix alerts if subscriptions drop to zero for more than a few minutes).
   - Orca: `task.invocations.duration` tracks queue task execution time; its count is critical since zero means Orca isn't processing new work (Spinnaker is "dead in the water" from a core behavior perspective).
   - Clouddriver: `cache.drift` tracks cache freshness (grouped by agent and region); `executionCount` tracks caching agent executions combined with status to identify failing agents. Some failures are acceptable as they often indicate downstream cloud provider issues.
   - Igor: `pollingMonitor.failed` tracks CI/SCM monitor poll failure rate (any value above 0 is bad, often due to downstream availability); `pollingMonitor.itemsOverThreshold` is a circuit breaker signal requiring manual intervention.

4. PRODUCT SLAs AT NETFLIX: Netflix tracks customer-specific metrics (e.g., cache read latency, ad-hoc pipeline execution reliability) and subscribes to customers' alerts to detect problems before customers report them.

5. OBSERVABILITY IMPROVEMENTS: The author highlights Spinnaker's gap in easily discoverable operational insights and suggests documenting metrics, their tags, purpose, and related alerts as a valuable contribution. A Special Interest Group exists at github.com/spinnaker/governance/tree/master/sig-ops for those interested in improving Spinnaker's operational characteristics.

# Monitoring

Each Spinnaker microservice is instrumented with numerous metrics exposed via a built in endpoint.

Each Spinnaker microservice is instrumented with numerous metrics exposed via a built in endpoint. The recommended approach for monitoring Spinnaker is to attach the [OpenTelemetry (OTEL) Java agent](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/zero-code/java/agent/) to each microservice via a Kubernetes init container, send telemetry to an [OpenTelemetry Collector](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/) , and configure that collector to forward data to your preferred monitoring backend.

> **Note on the Spinnaker Observability Plugin**: The Armory Observability Plugin (`armory-plugins/armory-observability-plugin`) was previously recommended but is no longer actively developed. New deployments should use the OTEL Java agent approach described on this page.

This approach provides:

* **Standard JVM metrics** (heap, GC, thread pools) auto-instrumented with no code changes
* **Spinnaker application metrics** via the agent’s built-in Micrometer extraction — no scraping required
* **Distributed tracing** across Spinnaker microservices
* **Vendor-neutral pipeline**: route the same telemetry to Prometheus, Datadog, New Relic, Grafana Cloud, or any OTLP-compatible backend by changing only the collector config

## Architecture Overview

```
Spinnaker microservices (OTEL Java agent injected via init container) │ │ OTLP (gRPC or HTTP) ▼ OpenTelemetry Collector │ ├──▶ Prometheus (remote write or scrape) ├──▶ Datadog ├──▶ New Relic └──▶ Any OTLP-compatible backend 
```

The OTEL Java agent includes built-in support for extracting [Micrometer](https://micrometer.io/) metrics from the JVM. Enabling this instrumentation causes the agent to collect Spinnaker’s internal application metrics and emit them via OTLP alongside standard JVM and HTTP metrics — no separate Prometheus scrape of `/spectator/metrics` is required.

## Step 1: Add the OTEL Agent as a Kustomize Component

The recommended way to inject the OTEL agent is as a [Kustomize component](https://github.com/spinnaker/spinnaker/tree/main/spinnaker-kustomize) that patches each service deployment to add an init container, a shared volume, and the required environment variables. This requires no changes to the base service images.

Create `components/otel-agent/kustomization.yml` in your spinnaker-kustomize directory:


The `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_MICROMETER_ENABLED=true` flag activates the agent’s built-in Micrometer instrumentation, which reads Spinnaker’s internal metrics at the JVM level and emits them via OTLP. No additional Spring or application config is needed.

> **Service names**: By default the agent uses the Deployment name as `service.name`. To set it explicitly per service, add individual per-deployment patches that set `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` (e.g. `clouddriver`, `orca`, `gate`).

```
components: components: components:  - components/otel-agent - components/otel-agent components/otel-agent  # ... other components # ... other components # ... other components  
```

```
kubectl kustomize -o spinnaker.yml kubectl kustomize -o spinnaker.yml kubectl apply -f spinnaker.yml kubectl apply -f spinnaker.yml 
```

## Consuming Metrics

### Spinnaker Application Metrics (Micrometer)

Spinnaker publishes internal metrics using a multi-dimensional data model based on “tags”. Each metric has a name and type; each data point is a numeric value time-stamped at the time of reporting and tagged with a set of one or more `label=value` pairs.

With `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_MICROMETER_ENABLED=true`, the OTEL agent reads these metrics directly from the JVM’s Micrometer registry and emits them via OTLP. See the [Monitoring Reference](/docs/reference/monitoring/) for a full description of available metrics, tags, and the data model.

### Types of Metrics

* **Counters** are monotonically increasing values over the lifetime of the process. Use counter differences over a time window to compute rates. Spinnaker also uses a special **Timer** counter type (always in nanoseconds) that emits complementary `__count` and `__totalTime` series. Divide `totalTime` by `count` to get average latency.
* **Gauges** are instantaneous value readings. Useful for queue sizes, active connections, and similar current-state measurements.

### Standard JVM Metrics (from OTEL agent)

The OTEL Java agent automatically emits:

* `jvm.memory.used` / `jvm.memory.committed` — heap and non-heap usage
* `jvm.gc.duration` — GC pause times
* `jvm.thread.count` — live threads
* `http.server.request.duration` — latency histogram for all HTTP endpoints
* `http.client.request.duration` — latency for outbound HTTP calls

These use [OpenTelemetry semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/) and are available in any backend without additional configuration.

args.summary:
This webpage documents the recommended approach for monitoring Spinnaker, the open-source continuous delivery platform. The recommended architecture is to attach the OpenTelemetry (OTEL) Java agent to each Spinnaker microservice via a Kubernetes init container, send telemetry to an OpenTelemetry Collector, and configure that collector to forward data to a preferred monitoring backend.

Key points:
- The Armory Observability Plugin (armory-plugins/armory-observability-plugin) is no longer actively developed and should be replaced by the OTEL Java agent approach.
- This approach provides: standard JVM metrics (heap, GC, thread pools) auto-instrumented with no code changes; Spinnaker application metrics via the agent's built-in Micrometer extraction (no scraping required); distributed tracing across Spinnaker microservices; and a vendor-neutral pipeline that can route telemetry to Prometheus, Datadog, New Relic, Grafana Cloud, or any OTLP-compatible backend by changing only the collector config.

Step-by-step instructions:
1. Add the OTEL agent as a Kustomize component (components/otel-agent/kustomization.yml) that patches each service deployment to add an init container (using image otel/autoinstrumentation-java:2.27.0), a shared volume, and environment variables including JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-javaagent:/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4317, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc, and OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_MICROMETER_ENABLED=true (which activates the agent's built-in Micrometer instrumentation to read Spinnaker's internal metrics at the JVM level, requiring no additional Spring or application config). Set OTEL_SERVICE_NAME per deployment (e.g., clouddriver, orca, gate). Enable the component in the root kustomization.yml and apply with kubectl kustomize.

2. Deploy the OpenTelemetry Collector as a standalone Deployment or DaemonSet that receives telemetry from agents and routes it to backends. Uses otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:latest image, exposing ports 4317 (OTLP gRPC), 4318 (OTLP HTTP), and 8888 (collector self-metrics). Config uses otlp receiver, batch and memory_limiter processors, and a prometheusremotewrite exporter.

3. Configure a backend by replacing the exporters section — options include Prometheus (remote write receiver with --web.enable-remote-write-receiver, or a scrape endpoint on port 8889), Datadog (API key and site datadoghq.com or .eu, requires contrib image), New Relic (otlp endpoint https://otlp.nr-data.net:4317 with api-key header), and Grafana Cloud (otlp endpoint with Basic authorization token). Multiple backends can be fanned out simultaneously.

Consuming metrics:
- Spinnaker publishes internal metrics using a multi-dimensional "tag"-based data model; each metric has a name/type and data points tagged with label=value pairs.
- Counters are monotonically increasing values (use differences over time for rates); Spinnaker uses a special Timer counter type in nanoseconds emitting complementary __count and __totalTime series (divide totalTime by count for average latency). Gauges provide instantaneous readings (queue sizes, active connections).
- The OTEL Java agent automatically emits jvm.memory.used/committed, jvm.gc.duration, jvm.thread.count, http.server.request.duration, and http.client.request.duration using OpenTelemetry semantic conventions.

Dashboards: The spinnaker-mixin project (github.com/uneeq-oss/spinnaker-mixin) provides pre-built Grafana dashboards for Prometheus-backed metrics, including per-microservice dashboards, cloud provider dashboards, and a Minimal Spinnaker overview.

The page was last modified August 13, 2026 (commit 4ae04c5). Spinnaker talks from cdCon 2026 are also available via YouTube playlist.

to Prometheus Developers

Hi All,

Prometheus has seen the fashion shifting from on-premise to clouds, monoliths to microservices, virtual machines to containers etc. Prometheus has proven to be successful for users in all those scenarios. Let's now talk about FaaS/Serverless. (Let's leave other buzzwords - blockchain/AI for later 🙈).

I would love to start a discussion around the usage of Prometheus Metrics on Serverless environments. I wonder if, from the Prometheus dev point of view, we can implement/integrate anything better, document or explain more etc. (:

**In this thread, I am specifically looking for:**

\* Existing best practices for using Prometheus for gathering metrics from Serverless/FaaS platforms and functions

\* Specific gaps and limitation users might have in these scenarios

\* Existing success stories?

\* Ideas for improvements.

**Action Item: Feel free to respond if you have any input on those!**

Past discussions:

\* [Fair suggestion to use cloud exporters for FaaS cases](https://groups.google.com/g/prometheus-users/c/_WSnJtn_TMw/m/f9Dh2cRkAQAJ)

\* Suggestion to use [event aggregation proxy](https://github.com/weaveworks/prom-aggregation-gateway)

\* [Pushgateway improvements](https://groups.google.com/g/prometheus-users/c/sm5qOrsVY80/m/nSfbzHd9AgAJ) for serverless cases

**My thoughts:**

IMO the FaaS function should be like function in any other full pledge application/pod. You programmatically increment common metric for your aggregated view (e.g overall number of errors).

Trying to switch to a push model for this case, sounds like an unnecessary complication because, in the end, those functions are running in the common, longer living context (e.g FaaS runtime). This runtime should give programmatic APIs to use custom metrics like it's possible in a normal app when your function has local variables (e.g \*prometheus.CounterVec) to use.

In fact, this is what AWS Lambda [allows](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/operating-lambda-logging-and-custom-metrics/)and there are [exporters to get that data](https://sysdig.com/blog/monitor-aws-lambda-prometheus/) into Prometheus.

We see users attempting to switch to the push model. I just wonder if for FaaS functions this really makes sense.

If you init the TCP connection and use remote write, OM push, pushgateway API / Otel/OpenCensus to push metric, you take enormous latency hit to spin up a new TCP connection just for that. This might be already too slow for FaaS. If you do this asynchronously on Faas platform, you need to care about discovery/backoffs/persistent buffer/auth and all pains of push model + some aggregation proxy like Pushgateway/Aggregation gateway or OTel collector to get this data to Prometheus (BTW this is what [knative is recommending](https://knative.dev/docs/install/collecting-metrics/)). Equally, one could just expose those metrics on /metrics endpoint and drop all of this complexity (or run exporter if FaaS is in the cloud, like Lambda/Google Run).

I think the main problem appears if those FaaS runtimes are short-living workloads that automatically spins up only to run some functions (batch jobs). In some way, this is then a problem of short-living jobs and the design of those workloads.

For those short-living jobs, we again see users try to use the push model. I think there is room to either streamline those initiatives OR propose an alternative. A quick idea, yolo... why not killing the job after the first successful scrape (detecting usage on /metric path)?

Kind Regards,

Bartek Płotka (@bwplotka)

to Bartłomiej Płotka, Prometheus Developers

On 15.06.21 20:59, Bartłomiej Płotka wrote:   
>   
> Let's now talk about FaaS/Serverless.

Excellent! That's my 2nd favorite topic after histograms. (And while I   
provably talked about histograms as my favorite topic since early   
2015, I have only started to talk about FaaS/Serverless as an   
important gap to fill in the Prometheus story since 2018.)   
   
I think "true FaaS" means that the function calls are   
lightweight. The additional overhead of sending anything over the   
networks defeats that purpose. So similar to what has been said   
before, and what Bartek has already nicely worked out, I think the   
metrics have to be managed by the FaaS runtime, in the same path as   
billing is managed.   
   
And that's, of course, what cloud providers are doing, and it's also a   
formidable way of locking their customers into their own metrics and   
monitoring system.   
   
And that's in turn precisely where I think Prometheus can use its   
weight. Prometheus has already proven that cloud providers can   
essentially not get away with ignoring it, and even halfhearted   
integrations won't be enough. With more or less native Prometheus   
support by cloud providers, it might actually just require a small   
step to come to some convention how to collect and present FaaS   
metrics in a "Promethean" way. If all cloud providers do it the same   
way, the lock-in is gone.   
   
I think it would be very valuable to study what OpenFaaS has already   
done: <https://docs.openfaas.com/architecture/metrics/>   
   
In the simplest case, we could just say: Please, dear cloud providers,   
please expose exactly the same metrics for general benefit. If there   
is anything to improve with the OpenFaaS approach, I'm sure they will   
be delighted to get help. (Spontaneously, I'm missing a way to define   
custom metrics, e.g. how many records a function call has processed.)   

> \* Suggestion to use event aggregation proxy

> <<https://github.com/weaveworks/prom-aggregation-gateway>>   
> \* Pushgateway improvements   
> <<https://groups.google.com/g/prometheus-users/c/sm5qOrsVY80/m/nSfbzHd9AgAJ>> for   
> serverless cases   
   
Despite all of what I said above, I think there \_are\_ quite a few user   
of FaaS who have fairly heavy-weight function calls. For them, pushing   
counter increments etc. via the network might actually be more   
convenient than funneling metrics through the FaaS runtime. This is   
then just another use-case of the "distributed counter" idea, which   
the Pushgateway quite prominently is not catering for. As discussed   
in the thread linked above and at countless other places, I strongly   
recommend to not shoehorn the Pushgateway into this use-case, but   
create a separate project for it, which would be designed from the   
beginning for this use-case. Perhaps   
weaveworks/prom-aggregation-gateway is just that. I haven't studied it   
in detail yet. In a way, we need "statsd done right". Again, I would   
suggest to look what others have already done. For example, there are   
tons of statsd users out there. What have they done in the last years   
to overcome the known shortcomings? Perhaps statsd instrumentation and   
the Prometheus statsd exporter just needs a bit of development in that   
way to make it a viable solution.   

> I think the main problem appears if those FaaS runtimes are short-living   
> workloads that automatically spins up only to run some functions (batch   
> jobs). In some way, this is then a problem of short-living jobs and the   
> design of those workloads.   
>   
> For those short-living jobs, we again see users try to use the push model.   
> I think there is room to either streamline those initiatives OR propose   
> an alternative. A quick idea, yolo... why not killing the job after the   
> first successful scrape (detecting usage on /metric path)?

Ugh, that doesn't sound right. I think this problem should be solved   
within the FaaS runtime in the way they prefer. Cloud providers need   
billing in any case (they want to make money after all), so they have   
already solved reliably metrics collection for that. They just need to   
hook in a simple exporter to present Prometheus metrics. See how   
OpenFaaS has done it. Knative seems to have gone down the OTel path,   
but that could be seen as an implementation detail. If they in the end   
expose a /metrics endpoint with the desired metrics for Prometheus to   
scrape, all is good. It's just a terribly overengineered exporter,   
effectively. (o;   
   
--   
Björn Rabenstein

Personally the reason I chose a serverless runtime (GCP Cloud Run) for my application layer is just in order to focus on business feature development. The runtime manages container lifecycles and we're only paying for the time containers serve traffic. I could deploy the exact same Docker container outside a serverless environment as well.  
My needs are still the same though: I want to instrument the various aspects of the service and its many endpoints, both with common request related metrics as well as custom metrics. The problem I face is the fundamental mismatch of Prometheus' pull architecture and the serverless runtime which doesn't even allow me to see individual container instances.  
  
The StatsD / push-over-network approach has some serious latency impact as you both highlighted already. Additionally, it requires the deployment of a service with an external TCP API which would need to be protected from public access as well (might be easy depending on the serverless runtime provider).  
  
Last night I was wondering if there are any other common interfaces available in serverless environments and noticed that all products by AWS (Lambda) and GCP (Functions, Run) at least provide the option to handle log streams, sometimes even log files on disk. I'm currently thinking about experimenting with an approach where containers log metrics to stdout / some file, get picked up by the serverless runtime and written to some log stream. Furthermore this approach requires some support by the client libraries (I think only the Ruby client supports custom data stores).

to Bartłomiej Płotka, Prometheus Developers

This has come up in the context of OM, OTel, and TAG Observability. My   
own thinking largely mirrors beorn's & grobie's: In a perfect world   
the orchestration layer has all the information and interfaces   
required and billing knows about the required datapaths, NB:   
Monitoring usually has higher speed and lower reliability requirements   
than billing. Still, for doability, lock-in, convenience, and velocity   
reasons, it's enticing to bypass the ideal solution and do something   
that works-ish now. If someone incurs ~100% overhead for monitoring   
lightweight functions but gets their job done, they are are still   
getting their job done and can optimize later if they so choose.   
   
Pushing might appear hamfisted here, and arguably is, but it's largely   
under the control of the dev; as such, they can do it with less   
coordination. This might get us near to using the Prometheus Agent as   
a Collector to reduce latency and blast radius. Far from ideal, but...   
   
An in-between would be what grobie said: To speak in Prometheus terms,   
the orchestrator is node\_exporter, the serverless functions write out   
something which the textfile collector can ingest.   
   
OpenMetrics deliberately supports push, but this approach creates   
issues with `up` and staleness handling. OTel is currently facing   
similar issues, maybe there's room for cooperation. Also see   
<https://github.com/OpenObservability/OpenMetrics/blob/main/specification/OpenMetrics.md#supporting-target-metadata-in-both-push-based-and-pull-based-systems>   
and <https://docs.google.com/document/d/1hn-u6WKLHxIsqYT1_u6eh94lyQeXrFaAouMshJcQFXs/edit#heading=h.e4p9f543e7i2>   
   
   
I strongly believe that we should be particular about the wire format;   
in a future in which orchestrators have a collector component, it   
would be nice to be able to simply expose the metrics for pulling or   
use PRW code and wire format.   
   
   
Best,   
Richard

>  a Collector to reduce latency and blast radius. Far from ideal, but...  
>    
>  An in-between would be what grobie said: To speak in Prometheus terms,  
>  the orchestrator is node\_exporter, the serverless functions write out  
>  something which the textfile collector can ingest.

There is not much overlap between the node\_exporter and the functionality needed here. It would need something which can read common log streams from major cloud providers / serverless runtimes, aggregate the logs, and then expose them. Only the last part is somewhat available in the node\_exporter and the rest doesn't really make sense there. Google's mtail would be a bit closer conceptually, but as we have full control over the clients and wire format there is no need for a full-fledged log parsing engine, and the cloud provider log reading part is still missing.

>  issues with `up` and staleness handling. OTel is currently facing  
>  similar issues, maybe there's room for cooperation. Also see

>  use PRW code and wire format.

Just to throw my 2c in, we've been battling with this problem at (company) as we move more services to a serverless model for our customer facing things. Chiefly the issue of metrics aggregation for services that can't easily track their own state across multiple requests. For us, there's just too many metric semantics for different aggregations than can be expressed in Prometheus types, so we have resorted to hacks such as <https://github.com/sinkingpoint/gravel-gateway> to be able to express these. The wider variety of OpenMetrics types solves most of these issues, but that requires push gateway support as above, and a non zero effort from clients to migrate to OpenMetrics client libs (if those even exist for their languages of choice).

For the above, \_we\_ answer the above in the following way:

> What tradeoff would it make when metric ingestion is slower than metric production? Backpressure or drop data?

Just drop it, with metrics to indicate as such

> What are the semantics of pushing a counter?

Aggregation by summing by default with different options available, configurable by the client

> Where would the data move from there, and how?

Exposed as per the push gateway as a regular Prometheus scrape

> How many of these receivers would you typically run? How much coordination is necessary between them?

This gets complicated. In our setup we have a daemonset in k8s and an ingress that does consistent hashing on the service name so that any given service is routed to two different instances

Having run this setup in production for about a year and a half now it works for us in practice although it's definitely not ideal. We'd welcome some sort of official OpenMetrics solution

- Colin

to Prometheus Developers

Hi all!   
  
Hope not too late for the discussion. I would like to revive it as I find it really useful for Knative and any serverless framework. As a Knative contributor, working also on the monitoring side of the project, here is my pov:

a) OpenFaas as an example (mentioned earlier above) might not be the best to consider as it seems that it only provides metrics  
at the ingress side (Gateway), similarly to what you get from a Service mesh like istio when you monitor its ingress.  
Don't see any option to collect user metrics at least out of the box. Another serverless system, Dapr, wrt tracing, has a sidecar that among others pushes traces to the OTEL collector  (<https://docs.dapr.io/operations/monitoring/tracing/open-telemetry-collector>). Although Dapr for metrics uses a pull model still this highlights the path they are taking. Knative btw supports different exporters and so it can either use a pull model or a push model. It is not restricted to opentelemetry at all.  
  
b) What is the targeted latency for serverless? In cloud environments it is possible to get invocation latency down to milliseconds (<https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/creating-low-latency-high-volume-apis-with-provisioned-concurrency>) for simple funcs and also minimize cold start issues. As a rule any solution that ship metrics should take far less than the func run and should not add considerable resource overhead. Also users depending on the cost model should not pay for that overhead and you need to be able to distinguish that somehow at least. Regarding latency some apps can tolerate seconds or even minutes of latency. So it depends on how people want to ship metrics given their scenario. Btw as a background info Knative cold start time is a few seconds (<https://groups.google.com/g/knative-users/c/vqkP95ibq60>).  
  
c) There is a question whether serverless runtime should provide metrics forwarding/collection. I would say it is possible for at least the end-to-end traffic metrics.This is for metrics related to requests entering the system eg. at ingress and usually each requests corresponds to a function invocation (Knative has this 1-1 mapping). Ingress seems the right point for robustness reasons. For example a request may fail at different stages and this is also true for Knative where different components may be on the request path. For any other metric including user metrics I would say that a different localized approach for gathering metrics seems preferable. Separation of concerns is one reason behind this as we dont want centralized components to become a metric sink like a collector while also doing other stuff like scaling apps etc.   
  
Looking at a possible generic solution, I would guess this to be based on a local agent. Afaik a local tcp connection is at that ms scale including time for sending a few kbs of metrics data. Of course this is not the only option, metrics could be written to some local file and then stream its contents (log solution mentioned above). Ideally an architecture that ships metrics locally to some agent on a node would roughly satisfy reqs (which should be captured btw in detail). That agent would then be possible to push metrics to a metrics collector with either via remote writing, if it is Prometheus based, or via some other way if it is OTEL node agent(<https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/main/docs/design.md#running-as-an-agent>) etc. This is already done elsewhere for example AWS (<https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Agent-open-telemetry.html>).  
  
Best,  
Stavros

This is a discussion thread from the Prometheus Developers Google Group (June 2021 - April 2022) on best practices and challenges for using Prometheus metrics in serverless/FaaS environments. The discussion was initiated by Bartłomiej Płotka (@bwplotka) of Red Hat.

## Key Discussion Points:

**Initial Post (Bartłomiej Płotka, Jun 15, 2021):** Płotka sought input on best practices, gaps, success stories, and improvement ideas for Prometheus metrics in serverless environments. His view: FaaS functions should behave like functions in any normal application/pod, incrementing common metrics programmatically in the longer-living FaaS runtime context. He cautioned against switching to push model for FaaS due to TCP connection latency hits, noting that exposing metrics on a /metrics endpoint avoids complexity. He acknowledged the main problem arises with short-living workloads (batch jobs) and jokingly proposed "killing the job after the first successful scrape."

**Bjoern Rabenstein (beorn):** Argued that for "true FaaS" (lightweight function calls), the overhead of network sends defeats the purpose, so metrics should be managed by the FaaS runtime (in the same path as billing). He noted cloud providers use this to lock customers into their own monitoring systems, but Prometheus could apply pressure for standardization. He recommended studying OpenFaaS's approach (docs.openfaas.com/architecture/metrics/) and noted a missing way to define custom metrics there. For heavy-weight FaaS calls, he acknowledged push-based network counter increments might be convenient but strongly recommended NOT shoehorning the Pushgateway into this use case — instead creating a separate project designed for it (perhaps weaveworks/prom-aggregation-gateway), essentially "statsd done right."

**Tobias Schmidt (GCP Cloud Run user):** Questioned whether there's a real difference between heavy/light-weight serverless vs traditional deployments. He chose serverless to focus on business features, not infrastructure. His problem: the fundamental mismatch of Prometheus's pull architecture with serverless runtimes that don't expose individual container instances. He proposed an experiment: containers logging metrics to stdout/log streams, which get picked up by serverless runtime, then a "loggateway" service aggregates them and exposes them on /metrics or pushes via remote write.

**Richard Hartmann:** Noted the orchestration layer (billing) has the required data paths, but monitoring has higher speed and lower reliability requirements than billing. He suggested the Prometheus Agent as a Collector to reduce latency and blast radius, and mentioned an in-between where orchestrator acts as node_exporter with serverless functions writing something the textfile collector can ingest. He stressed being particular about the wire format (OpenMetrics, PRW).

**Rob Skillington (M3):** Shared experience with OpenMetrics protobuf payload pushing used by short-running tasks (Jenkins, Flink jobs). He agreed pushing to a Prometheus Agent-like target supporting OpenMetrics push could be a good middle ground, proposing: (1) ability to specify multiple targets with quick failover (e.g., 5ms budget per target, 3 targets max = 15ms worst case), and (2) deduplication ability so retried pushes aren't double-counted (maybe via timestamping). He stressed it should be a "last resort" option with clear limitations.

**Matthias Rampke** asked about the ideal OpenMetrics push receiver properties: backpressure vs drop data tradeoff, counter push semantics, data movement, and receiver coordination.

**Colin Douch (Cloudflare):** Shared production experience battling metrics aggregation for serverless services that can't track their own state across requests. Used gravel-gateway (github.com/sinkingpoint/gravel-gateway) to express aggregations too complex for Prometheus types. Their answers: drop data with metrics indicating drops; sum aggregation by default with options; expose as regular Prometheus scrape; run as k8s daemonset with consistent hashing ingress routing services to two instances. Ran this in production ~1.5 years.

**Stavros Kontopoulos (Knative contributor, Jan 19, 2022):** (a) Noted OpenFaaS only provides ingress-side metrics (like service mesh), no user metrics out of box; Dapr has a sidecar pushing traces to OTel collector; Knative supports both pull and push models with different exporters. (b) Serverless invocation latency can be milliseconds (with provisioned concurrency), so metric shipping must take far less than function runtime without resource overhead. (c) Suggested serverless runtime should provide end-to-end traffic metrics (ingress is right point for robustness), while user metrics need a localized approach — ideally a local agent on the node (local TCP connection is millisecond-scale) that pushes via remote write or OTLP.

**Final Update (Płotka, Apr 5, 2022):** Mentioned two KubeCon EU talks: "Operating Prometheus in a Serverless World" (Colin Douch, Cloudflare) and "Fleeting Metrics: Monitoring Short-lived or Serverless Jobs with Prometheus" (Bartłomiej Płotka & Saswata Mukherjee, Red Hat). Also noted a meeting with the OpenFaaS community to gather feedback and requirements.

# Observability

## Table of contents

* [What is observability?](#h-what-is-observability)

## Table of contents

* [What is observability?](#h-what-is-observability)
* [Why observability matters](#h-why-observability-matters)
* [Observability vs. monitoring](#h-observability-vs-monitoring)
* [Observability in cloud-native environments](#h-observability-in-cloud-native-environments)
* [The role of observability in security](#h-the-role-of-observability-in-security)
* [Observability best practices](#h-observability-best-practices)
* [How Orca Security helps](#h-how-orca-security-helps)

Observability is the ability to measure, monitor, and understand the internal state of a system based on the data it produces—such as logs, metrics, and traces. Originally a control theory concept, observability in modern computing enables engineers and security teams to answer key questions about application behavior, performance, and reliability without needing direct access to the system’s internals.

In cloud-native, containerized, and distributed environments, observability is critical for diagnosing issues, ensuring uptime, optimizing performance, and detecting security incidents in real time.

## What is observability?

Observability refers to how well you can understand what’s happening inside a system from the outside. It is not just about collecting data—it’s about using that data to answer *why* something is happening, not just *what* is happening. This enables teams to investigate root causes, understand dependencies, and take proactive or corrective action quickly.

In practice, observability is achieved through the collection and correlation of three primary telemetry pillars:

**Logs**: Immutable, timestamped records of discrete events generated by applications, infrastructure, and services. Logs provide detailed context for what occurred at a specific point in time.

**Metrics**: Numeric measurements captured over time that quantify system health, usage, and performance (e.g., CPU usage, memory consumption, HTTP error rates). Metrics are typically aggregated and monitored for trends or thresholds.

**Traces**: End-to-end records of how a request moves through a system or service chain. Traces help identify bottlenecks, latency issues, or failures in distributed applications.

These three pillars are often supplemented with events, metadata, and topology information to provide a holistic view of system behavior.

## Why observability matters

Modern applications are complex, often built using microservices, serverless functions, containers, and APIs deployed across cloud and hybrid environments. Traditional monitoring tools fall short in these architectures because they focus on static metrics or predefined alerts without the context needed to troubleshoot dynamic, ephemeral systems.

Observability matters because it enables teams to:

* Detect and resolve performance issues faster by identifying root causes
* Improve user experience by reducing downtime and latency
* Understand the impact of changes or deployments in real time
* Monitor service dependencies and uncover cascading failures
* Detect anomalies or malicious activity that may indicate a security breach
* Support [SRE (Site Reliability Engineering](https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/sre/)) practices, SLAs, and error budgets
* Continuously improve systems through feedback loops and empirical data

Observability provides the insights needed to maintain reliability and resilience at scale.

## Observability vs. monitoring

While often used interchangeably, [observability and monitoring](https://aws.amazon.com/compare/the-difference-between-monitoring-and-observability/) are not the same:

**Monitoring** tells you when something is wrong—often through predefined dashboards and alerts based on known thresholds.

**Observability** helps you understand *why* it’s wrong—even in the face of unknown unknowns. It emphasizes the ability to ask new questions and explore telemetry in ways that weren’t anticipated during system design.

Monitoring is necessary but not sufficient for diagnosing complex problems. Observability adds the exploratory and diagnostic capability needed in dynamic environments where traditional assumptions don’t always apply.

## Observability in cloud-native environments

In cloud-native environments, observability is both more essential and more challenging. Containers, Kubernetes, and serverless functions create highly dynamic and short-lived components that require automated, scalable telemetry collection and analysis.

Key observability challenges in these environments include:

* **Ephemeral [workloads](https://orca.security/glossary/workload/)**: Containers may spin up and down in seconds, requiring real-time data collection and aggregation
* **Distributed traces**: A single user request may traverse dozens of microservices, requiring end-to-end visibility to trace failures
* **Multi-cloud complexity**: Organizations may run services across multiple providers, each with different telemetry standards and APIs
* **Security visibility**: Observability data is often the first indicator of compromise, making it valuable for detecting threats and anomalies
* **High data volume**: The sheer amount of telemetry generated can overwhelm systems without careful sampling, filtering, and prioritization

Tools and frameworks such as [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/), Prometheus, Fluentd, Jaeger, and Grafana are commonly used to collect, process, and visualize observability data in cloud-native systems.

## The role of observability in security

While traditionally viewed as a performance and reliability concern, observability is increasingly important in security operations. Observability data can help:

* Detect abnormal behavior, such as sudden spikes in resource usage or failed login attempts
* Correlate events across systems to identify [lateral movement](https://orca.security/glossary/lateral-movement/) or privilege escalation
* Reconstruct attack timelines using logs and traces
* Validate that cloud workloads and configurations comply with security policies
* Investigate data exfiltration, [malware](https://orca.security/glossary/malware/) activity, or insider threats
* Support forensics and [incident response](https://orca.security/glossary/incident-response/) through immutable, time-stamped data

Security observability bridges the gap between detection and response—helping teams move from passive monitoring to active threat hunting and resolution.

## Observability best practices

To build effective observability, organizations should:

* **Instrument early and often**: Integrate telemetry collection into code, infrastructure, and CI/CD pipelines
* **Correlate across data types**: Combine logs, metrics, and traces for full context rather than siloed insights
* **Use centralized platforms**: Aggregate data from disparate sources into a single observability platform for unified analysis
* **Set meaningful SLIs and SLOs**: Track service-level indicators and objectives that reflect user experience and business goals
* **Embrace open standards**: Use vendor-agnostic tools like OpenTelemetry to ensure portability and integration flexibility
* **Automate alerting**: Use machine learning and anomaly detection to surface unexpected issues faster
* **Protect sensitive data**: Ensure observability tools are configured to avoid leaking PII or exposing sensitive system details

Observability should be seen as a continuous discipline—evolving alongside application architecture and user needs.

## How Orca Security helps

The [Orca Cloud Security Platform](https://orca.security/platform/) enhances observability by providing deep comprehensive visibility across the multi-cloud environments of AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud, Alibaba Cloud, and Kubernetes.

With Orca, security and operations teams can:

* Analyze risks holistically to detect the root source of issues
* Surface the [attack paths](https://orca.security/resources/blog/cloud-attack-path-analysis/) that endanger high-value assets and [visualize cloud asset relationships](https://orca.security/resources/blog/graph-visualization-to-understand-interconnected-cloud-risks/) continuously and dynamically
* Scan and monitor cloud assets continuously for risks and threats, including [anomalies, suspicious activity, and potentially malicious behavior](https://orca.security/resources/blog/orca-enhances-cdr-capabilities/)
* [Prioritize remediation](https://orca.security/resources/blog/risk-based-vulnerability-management/) based on business impact and dynamic measures of criticality

By combining deep and comprehensive visibility with risk context, Orca enables teams to gain the cloud-native observability that supports effective risk prioritization and remediation.

**Scaling Guidelines:**
- Argo CD HA (High-availability) can comfortably support ~1,500 applications, 14,000 objects, 50 clusters, and 200 devs without tweaks.

- Security relies on RBAC and SSO; manifest rendering (Helm, Kustomize, JSonnet) is a potential risk area.

**Architecture Comparison:**

1. **Hub and Spoke**: Single Argo instance connects to many clusters. Pros: Easy management, simple access, simple DR. Cons: Single point of failure, lack of security isolation, Kubernetes APIs must be accessible. Best for small teams managing dev/staging/prod environments.

2. **Standalone**: Argo instance co-located with each cluster. Pros: Reliability, isolation. Cons: Management complexity, complex user access. Best for edge/air-gapped deployments, often paired with Crossplane or Terraform.

3. **Split-Instance**: Central management instance with components split across target clusters via tunnels. Pros: Secure connections to firewalled APIs, centralized config. Cons: Experimental, management complexity, limited community support.

4. **Control Plane**: Mix of standalone/hub-and-spoke with centralized management layer (e.g., Codefresh). Pros: Centralized config, zero-trust, independent upgrades, no single point of failure. Cons: Additional software to manage.

**Additional Recommendations:**
- Self-managed Argo CD is recommended for disaster recovery.
- Application configurations should be stored in git (not just created via UI).
- A control plane is recommended to simplify update/management overhead for multiple instances, as Argo CD versions have a lifespan shorter than a year (N-2 version support, quarterly releases).

--- SOURCE 15: Argo CD Architectures: Single vs. Per-Cluster vs. Hybrid - Akuity ---

<summary>
## Argo CD Architectures Explained: Single vs. Per-Cluster vs. Hybrid

This blog post from Akuity (published May 2025, updated July 2026 by Jesse Suen) compares four common Argo CD architectures for implementing GitOps on Kubernetes, focusing on how they affect scalability, security, operational overhead, and developer experience. The 2026 Argo CD User Survey found scaling and performance are now among the most cited challenges for teams running Argo CD at scale.

### The Four Architectures:

**1. Single Instance (Hub and Spoke)**
- One Argo CD instance runs on a dedicated management cluster and deploys to all other clusters remotely.
- **Best for:** Small teams, simple infrastructure, early Kubernetes adoption.
- **Advantages:** Single UI, API endpoint, and control plane; simple installation; strong ApplicationSet cluster generator integration.
- **Tradeoffs:** Single point of failure; centralized credential exposure (admin credentials for all clusters stored in one place); scaling requires manual tuning.
- **Security:** Recent improvements include RBAC narrowing to specific resources, mutual TLS, and automatic OIDC token refresh.

**2. Per Cluster (Dedicated Instance)**
- A full Argo CD instance runs inside every cluster and deploys only to that same cluster.
- **Best for:** Organizations prioritizing isolation and fault containment with strict security/compliance requirements.
- **Advantages:** Load distributed; no external API exposure needed; credentials scoped to single cluster; full fault isolation.
- **Tradeoffs:** Configuration duplication across instances; fragmented operator experience; ApplicationSet cluster generator not usable.

**3. Hybrid Architecture (Instance Per Logical Group)**
- One Argo CD instance per logical group of clusters (by team, region, or environment).
- **Best for:** Mid-sized organizations that outgrew single instance but lack platform headcount for per-cluster setup.
- **Advantages:** Load distributed across groups; blast radius contained per group; less duplication than per-cluster.

<summary>
# Argo Security Features, CVEs & Critical Security Practices

This article from Octopus Deploy provides a comprehensive overview of security features, vulnerabilities, and best practices for Argo CD, an open-source Continuous Delivery tool for Kubernetes that uses GitOps principles.

## Argo CD Security Features

- **Authentication**: Uses JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) instead of traditional username/password bearer tokens. Tokens expire after 24 hours. Local admin passwords stored as bcrypt hashes. Supports SSO via OIDC providers (including Dex) and automation tokens with limited, project-scoped privileges.
- **Authorization**: Employs its own RBAC system (separate from Kubernetes native RBAC). Policies consist of roles and rules, with granular permissions definable for different roles.
- **TLS**: Secures all network communications (external and internal). Can enforce TLS 1.2 via `--tlsminversion 1.2` flag. Redis communication over HTTP by default but TLS can be configured manually.
- **Repository Management**: Uses a dedicated `repo-server` service with no Kubernetes permissions or stored credentials. Supports Helm and Kustomize, though these introduce risks if repositories are compromised.
- **Sensitive Information**: Credentials and secrets are never returned in API responses and are always redacted from logs. Cluster credentials stored as Kubernetes secrets. For Kubernetes 1.24+, non-expiring ServiceAccount tokens are created; token rotation is manual.
- **Cluster RBAC**: Default cluster admin role can be restricted to specific namespaces or resource types. Resources can be excluded entirely from Argo CD's management scope.
- **Auditing**: Git commit history provides built-in auditability. Argo CD emits Kubernetes Events tracking application-related activities. Long-term retention requires external tools like Event Exporter or Event Router.
- **Logging**: Logs tagged with "security" field, categorized into five severity levels (Low to Emergency). Sensitive information is not logged during session creation or cluster operations.

## Past Security Vulnerabilities

1. **CVE-2020-1747 / CVE-2020-14343**: PyYAML code execution (fixed in v1.5.8)
2. **CVE-2020-5260**: Git credential leak (fixed in v1.4.3 / v1.5.2)
3. **CVE-2020-11576**: User enumeration (fixed in v1.5.1)
4. **CVE-2020-8828**: Insecure default admin password using pod name (fixed in v1.8.0)
5. **CVE-2020-8827**: Insufficient anti-brute force measures (fixed in v1.5.3)
6. **CVE-2020-8826**: Session fixation (mitigated via regular password changes)
7. **CVE-2018-21034**: Sensitive information disclosure (fixed in v1.5.0)

## Best Practices

1. Use a dedicated project for the control plane, isolating it from other applications.
2. Restrict management of argoproj.io API resources (Application, ApplicationSet) to Argo CD administrators only.
3. Block ClusterRoleBindings in most projects to prevent privilege escalation.
4. Narrow roles on remote clusters using dedicated service accounts with limited permissions.
5. Use RBAC in multi-tenant environments with custom roles and project-specific policies.
6. Maintain a CVE response plan, monitoring GitHub security advisories and reviewing audit logs.

## Additional Tips from the Author (Kostis Kapelonis, Principal Developer Advocate at Octopus Deploy)

- Use network policies for inter-component security
- Automate security configuration checks with OPA or Kyverno
- Configure IP allowlists on external access
- Implement secrets rotation and monitoring
- Isolate Helm/Kustomize operations with sandboxing

- **Auditing**: Git commit history provides natural audit logging, supplemented by Kubernetes Events that track application activity and actor identity.

- **Webhook Payloads**: Webhook payloads are treated as untrusted and only used to trigger application refresh for reconciliation.

<summary>
This webpage documents the Argo CD release process and cadence, outlining the schedule and procedures for upcoming minor and patch releases.

**Release Schedule (upcoming releases as of Aug 2026):**
- v3.6: RC1 on Sep. 15, 2026; GA on Nov. 3, 2026 (Champion: Eugene Doudine)
- v3.5: RC1 on Jun. 16, 2026; GA on Aug. 4, 2026 (Champion: Patroklos Papapetrou; Approver: Regina Voloshin)
- v3.4: RC1 on Mar. 16, 2026; GA on May. 5, 2026 (Champion: Codey Jenkins; Approver: Regina Voloshin)
- v3.3: RC1 on Dec. 15, 2025; GA on Feb. 2, 2026 (Champion: Peter Jiang; Approver: Regina Voloshin)
- Plus historical releases from v3.2 back to v2.6, each with named Champions and Approvers.

**Release Process:**
- **Minor Releases (2.x.0):** Occur four times a year (once every three months). Each GA release is preceded by several Release Candidates (RCs), with the first RC released seven weeks before the scheduled GA date, creating a seven-week feature freeze.
- **Patch Releases (2.5.x):** Occur on an as-needed basis. Only the three most recent minor versions are eligible for patch releases. Older versions are considered End-of-Life (EOL) and receive no bug fixes or security updates.

**Release Champion:** A community member responsible for a checklist of items (an issue template in the Argo CD repository) for each release. Some tasks (cherry-picking bug fixes, cutting releases) require Approver membership, which the Champion can delegate to.

**Other Policies:**
- **Feature Acceptance Criteria:** Features must meet criteria before the RC date to be included in a minor release. Large features need a reviewed and merged Proposal. Features not meeting criteria must wait for the next minor release.
- **Security Patch Policy:** CVEs in Argo CD code are patched for all supported versions.
- **Dependencies Lifecycle Policy:** Dependencies are evaluated to ensure they are actively maintained and maintained by trustworthy maintainers. Deprecated or unmaintained dependencies are scheduled for removal. CVEs in dependencies are patched for all supported versions if assessed by Snyk as high or critical severity.
- **Helm and Kustomize Upgrades:** Bundled Helm and Kustomize are upgraded to the latest versions at the start of each minor release cycle, with breaking changes documented in upgrade instructions.
- **Go Version Upgrades:** The Go version is upgraded to the latest at the start of each minor release cycle (in GOLANG_VERSION and go-version). The go.mod version should only be bumped if new language features are needed, to avoid forcing library users to upgrade their Go versions.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from OneUptime, published February 26, 2026, by Nawaz Dhandala, provides a comprehensive guide on managing Kubernetes secrets using ArgoCD with the External Secrets Operator (ESO). Unlike sealed secrets which encrypt secrets in Git, ESO pulls secrets from external secret stores at runtime, with Git repositories containing only references (ExternalSecret custom resources) rather than the actual secret values.

The guide covers:
1. **How ESO works**: The ExternalSecret CR defines which secrets to fetch and from where; the ESO controller continuously syncs secrets from external stores (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) into Kubernetes Secrets.

2. **Installation**: Deploy ESO via an ArgoCD Application using the external-secrets Helm chart (targetRevision 2.5.0) with installCRDs and automation settings.

3. **Configuring Secret Stores**: Includes detailed YAML examples for:
   - AWS Secrets Manager (using static IAM credentials or IRSA/JWT auth for EKS)
   - HashiCorp Vault (Kubernetes auth)
   - Azure Key Vault (Workload Identity)
   - Google Secret Manager (Workload Identity)

4. **Creating ExternalSecrets**: YAML examples showing how to define ExternalSecret resources (safe for Git since they only contain references), including refreshInterval settings and secret key mapping.

5. **ArgoCD Integration**: 
   - Recommended repository structure with base/overlays pattern
   - Use of sync waves (annotation `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-2"`) to ensure secrets are fetched before application deployment
   - A custom ArgoCD health check (Lua script in argocd-cm ConfigMap) to wait until ExternalSecrets report Ready status

6. **Handling Secret Diffs**: Use `ignoreDifferences` with jsonPointers on `/data` to prevent ArgoCD from showing externally-managed secrets as OutOfSync.

7. **Fetching multiple secrets**: Using `dataFrom` with `extract` (all properties) or `find` with regex for discovering secrets.

8. **Monitoring/troubleshooting commands**: kubectl commands for checking ExternalSecret status, ESO controller logs, and verifying generated Kubernetes secrets.

The article concludes that ESO is the best choice when a centralized secret management system already exists, as it keeps actual secret values out of Git, centralizes management, and uses refreshInterval to synchronize rotated secrets. Combined with ArgoCD's sync waves and custom health checks, it enables a fully GitOps-driven workflow. Alternative approaches reference guides on Sealed Secrets and SOPS with ArgoCD. 1. **Sealed Secrets**: Uses a custom resource (sealed secret) stored in Git; kubeseal tool retrieves encryption key from cluster; manual encryption required; no external dependencies; best for small numbers of clusters/secrets or quick starts.

3. **SOPS (Secrets Operations)**: Uses key stores instead of secret managers; requires manual encryption of every secret; stored in Git; needs a SOPS plugin for Argo CD; described as "solving a problem that doesn't exist anymore" and best used "in 2018" — many still use it due to tradition.

5. **Secret Store CSI**: Container Storage Interface driver runs on each Kubernetes node (daemon set); not per-pod based; doesn't watch for secret updates (only updates on volume creation/pod start); doesn't create Kubernetes secrets by default; can connect to multiple secrets managers.
6. **External Secrets**: Utilizes custom resources with a controller watching them; controller uses a cluster secret store for credentials; can connect to multiple sources including other Kubernetes clusters; supports templates; can update secrets silently (pods may need restart); the presenters recommend it as the winner and say "if you don't have time to research your solution, just choose external secrets."

Q&A highlights: security comparison (Kubernetes secrets can be managed with RBAC; Vault Agent preferred only if avoiding Kubernetes secrets), sealed secrets disaster recovery (decryption keys can be copied between clusters to avoid re-encryption), external secrets storage locations (in external managers like Vault, AWS, Google), and authentication solutions for HashiCorp Vault (JWT tokens from Kubernetes users). **Local Users/Accounts:**
- Argo CD has one built-in `admin` user with full system access; recommended for initial configuration only.
- Local users are defined in the `argocd-cm` ConfigMap using entries like `accounts.alice: apiKey, login` (each user can have apiKey and/or login capabilities).

- Failed login rate limiting is controlled by environment variables: `ARGOCD_SESSION_FAILURE_MAX_FAIL_COUNT` (default 5), `ARGOCD_SESSION_FAILURE_WINDOW_SECONDS` (default 300 seconds), `ARGOCD_SESSION_MAX_CACHE_SIZE` (default 1000), and `ARGOCD_MAX_CONCURRENT_LOGIN_REQUESTS_COUNT` (default 50).

- **Token Revocation**: Argo CD implements server-side token revocation on logout for enhanced security; the `argocd logout` command degrades gracefully when the server is unreachable. Security best practices include short-lived tokens, enabling logout URLs, and monitoring token usage.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a transcript of "GitOps Guide to the Galaxy (Ep 16): Using RBAC with ArgoCD," a Red Hat YouTube show hosted by Christian Hernandez and Chris Short, posted June 4, 2021. The episode covers how role-based access control (RBAC) works with Argo CD, particularly in the context of OpenShift and multi-tenant clusters.

Key topics covered:
- Argo CD is an open source, declarative, GitOps continuous delivery tool that automates deployment of services in Kubernetes environments.
- Core Argo CD concepts: An "Application" is a CRD representing a logical collection of manifests (could be simple like pod/service/route, or complex like full application deployments). An Argo CD "Project" is a logical grouping of applications used for multi-tenant isolation (team A can see project Foo, team B sees project Bar in the same Argo instance without knowing about each other).
- Argo CD has only two built-in roles: read-only and 100% admin (all or nothing). Any other roles must be custom-built.
- RBAC policies are written in a format: P (policy), role/user/group, resource (clusters, projects, applications, repositories), action (get, update, sync, create, delete), and specific target.
