*Author:* [*Andy Glover*](https://twitter.com/aglover)

Since releasing [Spinnaker](https://www.spinnaker.io/) to the [open source community in 2015](https://medium.com/netflix-techblog/global-continuous-delivery-with-spinnaker-2a6896c23ba7), the platform has flourished with the addition of new cloud providers, triggers, pipeline stages, and much more. Myriad new features, improvements, and innovations have been added by an ever growing, actively engaged community. Each new innovation has been a step towards an even better Continuous Delivery platform that facilitates rapid, reliable, [safe delivery](https://medium.com/netflix-techblog/automated-canary-analysis-at-netflix-with-kayenta-3260bc7acc69) of flexible assets to pluggable deployment targets.

![]()

Over the last year, Netflix has improved overall management of Spinnaker by enhancing community engagement and transparency. At the [Spinnaker Summit](https://www.spinnakersummit.com/) in 2018, we announced that we had adopted a formalized [project governance](https://www.spinnaker.io/community/governance/) plan with Google. Moreover, we also realized that we’ll need to share the responsibility of Spinnaker’s direction as well as yield a level of long-term strategic influence over the project so as to maintain a healthy, engaged community. This means enabling more parties outside of Netflix and Google to have a say in the direction and implementation of Spinnaker.

## Get Netflix Technology Blog’s stories in your inbox

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Remember me for faster sign in

A strong, healthy, committed community benefits everyone; however, open source projects rarely reach this critical mass. It’s clear Spinnaker has reached this special stage in its evolution; accordingly, we are thrilled to announce two exciting developments.

First, Netflix and Google are jointly donating Spinnaker to the newly created [Continuous Delivery Foundation (or CDF)](https://cd.foundation/), which is part of the Linux Foundation. The CDF is a neutral organization that will grow and sustain an open continuous delivery ecosystem, much like the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (or CNCF) has done for the cloud native computing ecosystem. The initial set of projects to be donated to the CDF are Jenkins, Jenkins X, Spinnaker, and Tekton. Second, Netflix is joining as a founding member of the CDF. Continuous Delivery powers innovation at Netflix and working with other leading practitioners to promote Continuous Delivery through specifications is an exciting opportunity to join forces and bring the benefits of rapid, reliable, and safe delivery to an even larger community.

Spinnaker’s success is in large part due to the amazing community of companies and people that use it and contribute to it. Donating Spinnaker to the CDF will strengthen this community. This move will encourage contributions and investments from additional companies who are undoubtedly waiting on the sidelines. Opening the doors to new companies increases the innovations we’ll see in Spinnaker, which benefits everyone.

Donating Spinnaker to the CDF doesn’t change Netflix’s commitment to Spinnaker, and what’s more, current users of Spinnaker are unaffected by this change. Spinnaker’s previously defined governance policy remains in place. Overtime, new stakeholders will emerge and play a larger, more formal role in shaping Spinnaker’s future. The prospects of an even healthier and more engaged community focused on Spinnaker and the manifold benefits of Continuous Delivery is tremendously exciting and we’re looking forward to seeing it continue to flourish.

<summary>
This blog post from OneUptime (dated Feb 26, 2026) provides a detailed technical comparison of Argo Rollouts and Flagger for progressive delivery on Kubernetes. Progressive delivery is the practice of gradually rolling out changes to users for safe production releases.

**Key Architectural Difference:** Argo Rollouts replaces the standard Kubernetes Deployment resource with a custom `Rollout` resource, giving more fine-grained control. Flagger adds a `Canary` custom resource around existing Deployments without replacing the workload type, making it less invasive.

**Canary Deployments:** Argo Rollouts uses explicit, user-defined steps with precise control over each phase. Flagger uses declarative analysis specs with automatic step progression, increasing traffic by `stepWeight` at each `interval` as long as metrics pass.

**Blue-Green Deployments:** Both support blue-green deployments. Argo Rollouts uses a dedicated `blueGreen` strategy with active/preview services and optional pre-promotion analysis. Flagger's blue-green mode is triggered when no `stepWeight`/`maxWeight` is set.

**Analysis and Metrics:** Argo Rollouts supports Prometheus, Datadog, NewRelic, Wavefront, CloudWatch, Graphite, InfluxDB, Kayenta, Apache SkyWalking, Kubernetes Jobs, and web-based metrics. **Traffic Management:** Both support Istio, Linkerd, Nginx Ingress, SMI, Apache APISIX, and Traefik. Argo Rollouts additionally supports AWS ALB but not Contour or Gloo (which Flagger supports).

**GitOps Integration:** Argo Rollouts integrates tightly with ArgoCD (built-in health checks, actions, and UI extension). Flagger works natively with FluxCD but also with ArgoCD (with some configuration to avoid resource conflicts).

**Rollback Behavior:** Both automatically revert to stable versions when analysis fails.

**When to Choose Argo Rollouts:** Already using ArgoCD, want step-by-step control, need advanced features (experiments, header-based routing), use AWS ALB/Traefik, or want a dedicated CRD.

**When to Choose Flagger:** Prefer standard Kubernetes Deployments, use FluxCD, want a less invasive approach, use Contour/Gloo, or need webhook-based testing integrated into the rollout process.

<summary>
This blog post by Scott Rigby (published January 26, 2024 on Buoyant's website) compares progressive delivery tools and strategies for Kubernetes, with a focus on Flagger vs Argo Rollouts and the role of service meshes like Linkerd.

**Progressive Delivery Concepts:** Progressive delivery rolls out new application versions incrementally, evaluating success at each step before full deployment. It uses metrics like error thresholds, latency, and SLOs/SLAs to determine if a release meets standards.

**Deployment Strategies Covered:**
- **Canary Release:** Progressive traffic shifting by percentage from old to new version with analysis and rollback capability.
- **A/B Testing (Experiments):** Select user groups stay on the new version using HTTP header matching or cookies (session affinity).
- **Blue/Green:** Testing with simulated traffic, then switching live traffic all at once; old version kept for rollback.

**Service Mesh Role:** A service mesh like Linkerd is optional but adds capabilities: session affinity for canary releases and traffic mirroring for blue/green deployments.

**SMI vs Gateway API:** The Service Mesh Interface (SMI) project is now archived; the CNCF recommends adopting Gateway API (v1.0 GA as of October 2023) for service mesh networking, including east/west traffic. Both Flagger and Argo Rollouts support Gateway API.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Octopus provides a comprehensive overview of Argo CD deployment architectures for scaling Kubernetes management. It covers four main architectures: Hub and Spoke, Standalone, Split-Instance, and Control Plane, along with guidelines for scaling across performance, security, usability, and failover dimensions.

**Scaling Guidelines:**
- Argo CD HA (High-availability) can comfortably support ~1,500 applications, 14,000 objects, 50 clusters, and 200 devs without tweaks.
- Performance is aided by Redis caching; HA deploys minimum 3 Redis replicas across 3 nodes.
- Security relies on RBAC and SSO; manifest rendering (Helm, Kustomize, JSonnet) is a potential risk area.
- Failover concerns center on "blast radius" — the maximum scope of catastrophic failures.

**Architecture Comparison:**

1. **Hub and Spoke**: Single Argo instance connects to many clusters. Pros: Easy management, simple access, simple DR. Cons: Single point of failure, lack of security isolation, Kubernetes APIs must be accessible. Best for small teams managing dev/staging/prod environments.

2. **Standalone**: Argo instance co-located with each cluster. Pros: Reliability, isolation. Cons: Management complexity, complex user access. Best for edge/air-gapped deployments, often paired with Crossplane or Terraform.

3. **Split-Instance**: Central management instance with components split across target clusters via tunnels. Pros: Secure connections to firewalled APIs, centralized config. Cons: Experimental, management complexity, limited community support.

4. **Control Plane**: Mix of standalone/hub-and-spoke with centralized management layer (e.g., Codefresh). Pros: Centralized config, zero-trust, independent upgrades, no single point of failure. Cons: Additional software to manage.

**Additional Recommendations:**
- Self-managed Argo CD is recommended for disaster recovery.
- Application configurations should be stored in git (not just created via UI).
- A control plane is recommended to simplify update/management overhead for multiple instances, as Argo CD versions have a lifespan shorter than a year (N-2 version support, quarterly releases).
</summary>

## Argo CD Architectures Explained: Single vs. Per-Cluster vs. Hybrid

This blog post from Akuity (published May 2025, updated July 2026 by Jesse Suen) compares four common Argo CD architectures for implementing GitOps on Kubernetes, focusing on how they affect scalability, security, operational overhead, and developer experience. The 2026 Argo CD User Survey found scaling and performance are now among the most cited challenges for teams running Argo CD at scale.

### The Four Architectures:

**1. Single Instance (Hub and Spoke)**
- One Argo CD instance runs on a dedicated management cluster and deploys to all other clusters remotely.
- **Best for:** Small teams, simple infrastructure, early Kubernetes adoption.
- **Advantages:** Single UI, API endpoint, and control plane; simple installation; strong ApplicationSet cluster generator integration.
- **Tradeoffs:** Single point of failure; centralized credential exposure (admin credentials for all clusters stored in one place); scaling requires manual tuning.
- **Security:** Recent improvements include RBAC narrowing to specific resources, mutual TLS, and automatic OIDC token refresh.

**2. Per Cluster (Dedicated Instance)**
- A full Argo CD instance runs inside every cluster and deploys only to that same cluster.
- **Best for:** Organizations prioritizing isolation and fault containment with strict security/compliance requirements.
- **Advantages:** Load distributed; no external API exposure needed; credentials scoped to single cluster; full fault isolation.
- **Tradeoffs:** Configuration duplication across instances; fragmented operator experience; ApplicationSet cluster generator not usable.

**3. Hybrid Architecture (Instance Per Logical Group)**
- One Argo CD instance per logical group of clusters (by team, region, or environment).
- **Best for:** Mid-sized organizations that outgrew single instance but lack platform headcount for per-cluster setup.
- **Advantages:** Load distributed across groups; blast radius contained per group; less duplication than per-cluster.
- **Tradeoffs:** Still requires managing multiple instances; each group needs a management cluster; group-level ApplicationSet must be duplicated per group.

**4. Akuity Platform Agent-Based Approach (Enterprise Scale)**
- An agent runs inside each managed cluster with outbound-only access to the control plane.
- **Best for:** Enterprise fleets needing central visibility with in-cluster control.
- **Advantages:** Tested at 50,000 applications and 1,000 clusters; no external cluster access required; automatic disaster recovery; built-in audit logging.
- **Tradeoffs:** SaaS cost; less control of underlying hosting.
- **Key differentiator:** Reverses connection direction (agents connect outbound), removing need to expose cluster API servers or store admin credentials centrally.

### How to Choose:
The decision depends on team size, security requirements, platform engineering capacity, and pace of growth. The structural comparison table summarizes: instance count, whether a management cluster is required, external cluster access needed, configuration duplication, blast radius, and ApplicationSet cluster generator support.

<summary>
# Argo Security Features, CVEs & Critical Security Practices

This article from Octopus Deploy provides a comprehensive overview of security features, vulnerabilities, and best practices for Argo CD, an open-source Continuous Delivery tool for Kubernetes that uses GitOps principles.

## Argo CD Security Features

- **Authentication**: Uses JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) instead of traditional username/password bearer tokens. Tokens expire after 24 hours. Local admin passwords stored as bcrypt hashes. Supports SSO via OIDC providers (including Dex) and automation tokens with limited, project-scoped privileges.
- **Authorization**: Employs its own RBAC system (separate from Kubernetes native RBAC). Policies consist of roles and rules, with granular permissions definable for different roles.
- **TLS**: Secures all network communications (external and internal). Can enforce TLS 1.2 via `--tlsminversion 1.2` flag. Redis communication over HTTP by default but TLS can be configured manually.
- **Repository Management**: Uses a dedicated `repo-server` service with no Kubernetes permissions or stored credentials. Supports Helm and Kustomize, though these introduce risks if repositories are compromised.
- **Sensitive Information**: Credentials and secrets are never returned in API responses and are always redacted from logs. Cluster credentials stored as Kubernetes secrets. For Kubernetes 1.24+, non-expiring ServiceAccount tokens are created; token rotation is manual.
- **Cluster RBAC**: Default cluster admin role can be restricted to specific namespaces or resource types. Resources can be excluded entirely from Argo CD's management scope.
- **Auditing**: Git commit history provides built-in auditability. Argo CD emits Kubernetes Events tracking application-related activities. Long-term retention requires external tools like Event Exporter or Event Router.
- **Logging**: Logs tagged with "security" field, categorized into five severity levels (Low to Emergency). Sensitive information is not logged during session creation or cluster operations.

## Past Security Vulnerabilities

1. **CVE-2020-1747 / CVE-2020-14343**: PyYAML code execution (fixed in v1.5.8)
2. **CVE-2020-5260**: Git credential leak (fixed in v1.4.3 / v1.5.2)
3. **CVE-2020-11576**: User enumeration (fixed in v1.5.1)
4. **CVE-2020-8828**: Insecure default admin password using pod name (fixed in v1.8.0)
5. **CVE-2020-8827**: Insufficient anti-brute force measures (fixed in v1.5.3)
6. **CVE-2020-8826**: Session fixation (mitigated via regular password changes)
7. **CVE-2018-21034**: Sensitive information disclosure (fixed in v1.5.0)

## Best Practices

1. Use a dedicated project for the control plane, isolating it from other applications.
2. Restrict management of argoproj.io API resources (Application, ApplicationSet) to Argo CD administrators only.
3. Block ClusterRoleBindings in most projects to prevent privilege escalation.
4. Narrow roles on remote clusters using dedicated service accounts with limited permissions.
5. Use RBAC in multi-tenant environments with custom roles and project-specific policies.
6. Maintain a CVE response plan, monitoring GitHub security advisories and reviewing audit logs.

## Additional Tips from the Author (Kostis Kapelonis, Principal Developer Advocate at Octopus Deploy)

- Use network policies for inter-component security
- Automate security configuration checks with OPA or Kyverno
- Configure IP allowlists on external access
- Implement secrets rotation and monitoring
- Isolate Helm/Kustomize operations with sandboxing
</summary>

This article compares ArgoCD and FluxCD, the two leading GitOps tools for Kubernetes, as of 2026. ArgoCD 3.3 and Flux 2.8 represent the latest versions of each tool.

**Architectural Differences:** ArgoCD uses a centralized hub-and-spoke model with a management cluster controlling multiple clusters, providing a unified dashboard but concentrating credentials and increasing blast radius. FluxCD uses a decentralized toolkit approach with per-cluster controllers, operating with minimal resource overhead and no inbound network requirements—ideal for edge computing.

**ArgoCD 3.3 Key Features:** Introduces PreDelete hooks for safe application deletion, OIDC background token refresh, shallow cloning for monorepo fetch times (reducing from minutes to seconds), and Git Notes-based source hydration to reduce commit noise. It supports up to 50,000 apps per instance with tuning, using Redis sharding and controller sharding.

**Flux 2.8 Key Features:** Introduces a new Flux Web UI with OIDC/RBAC integration, native Helm v4 support with Server-Side Apply (SSA), kstatus-based health checking, CEL-based health expressions, and interruptible reconciliation that cancels ongoing health checks when a fix is detected—reducing MTTR. Flux uses the Helm SDK natively, making Helm releases visible via standard `helm list` commands.

**Helm Handling Divergence:** ArgoCD treats Helm as a manifest generator (helm template approach), losing native Helm lifecycle management. FluxCD uses the Helm SDK natively, supporting full Helm hooks, rollbacks, and post-rendering with Kustomize.

**Security:** ArgoCD has its own sophisticated RBAC with SSO integration (Dex, OIDC, SAML) and application-level granularity. FluxCD relies on standard Kubernetes RBAC with a minimal attack surface and no exposed API server by default.

**AI Integration (Agentic GitOps):** Flux offers an MCP Server for AI assistants to interact with clusters. ArgoCD's rich API and notification system support AI-driven remediation plugins, with KEDA integration for autonomous correction loops.

**Industry Recommendations:** ArgoCD is recommended for fintech (compliance/audit), retail/e-commerce (speed & visibility), and centralized platform teams. FluxCD is recommended for manufacturing edge computing, telecommunications (network isolation), and SaaS startups (automation-first, low overhead).

**Progressive Delivery:** ArgoCD uses Argo Rollouts (replaces Deployment with Rollout CRD). FluxCD uses Flagger (manages canary alongside primary, manipulates service meshes).

**The article concludes that the choice depends on organizational topology, resource constraints, developer experience preferences, and integration requirements—not which tool is "better."**
</summary>

- **Minor Releases (2.x.0):** Occur four times a year (once every three months). Each GA release is preceded by several Release Candidates (RCs), with the first RC released seven weeks before the scheduled GA date, creating a seven-week feature freeze.
- **Patch Releases (2.5.x):** Occur on an as-needed basis. Only the three most recent minor versions are eligible for patch releases. Older versions are considered End-of-Life (EOL) and receive no bug fixes or security updates.

**Release Champion:** A community member responsible for a checklist of items (an issue template in the Argo CD repository) for each release. Some tasks (cherry-picking bug fixes, cutting releases) require Approver membership, which the Champion can delegate to.

**Other Policies:**
- **Feature Acceptance Criteria:** Features must meet criteria before the RC date to be included in a minor release. Large features need a reviewed and merged Proposal. Features not meeting criteria must wait for the next minor release.
- **Security Patch Policy:** CVEs in Argo CD code are patched for all supported versions.
- **Dependencies Lifecycle Policy:** Dependencies are evaluated to ensure they are actively maintained and maintained by trustworthy maintainers. Deprecated or unmaintained dependencies are scheduled for removal. CVEs in dependencies are patched for all supported versions if assessed by Snyk as high or critical severity.
- **Helm and Kustomize Upgrades:** Bundled Helm and Kustomize are upgraded to the latest versions at the start of each minor release cycle, with breaking changes documented in upgrade instructions.
- **Go Version Upgrades:** The Go version is upgraded to the latest at the start of each minor release cycle (in GOLANG_VERSION and go-version). The go.mod version should only be bumped if new language features are needed, to avoid forcing library users to upgrade their Go versions.

**Metrics Cache Expiration**: For environments with heavy application/project churn, the `--metrics-cache-expiration` flag (e.g., `"--metrics-cache-expiration=\"24h0m0s\""`) can be used to schedule a metrics reset to reduce cardinality.

**Exposing Application/Cluster labels as metrics**: Disabled by default. Can be enabled by setting `controller.metrics.application.labels`, `controller.metrics.application.conditions`, or `controller.metrics.cluster.labels` keys in the `argocd-cmd-params-cm` ConfigMap, or by passing `--metrics-application-labels`, `--metrics-application-conditions`, and `--metrics-cluster-labels` flags to the controller. A warning notes that each distinct label value creates a new time series, increasing cardinality and degrading Prometheus performance.

**Application Set Controller Metrics**: Includes `argocd_appset_info`, `argocd_appset_reconcile`, `argocd_appset_labels` (disabled by default, enabled via `–metrics-applicationset-labels` argument), `argocd_appset_owned_applications`, plus kubectl metrics. **Repo Server Metrics** (scraped at `argocd-repo-server:8084/metrics`): Includes git request metrics, git fetch failures, Redis request metrics, repo parallelism wait duration, and OCI-related metrics (requests, duration, test repo/gat tags/digest metadata/resolve revision/extract failures).

This is a OneUptime blog post (by @nawazdhandala, dated Feb 02, 2026, technically validated Jun 10, 2026) providing a comprehensive technical guide on implementing Single Sign-On (SSO) for ArgoCD using Dex as an identity broker. ArgoCD includes Dex as its built-in OIDC provider.

**SSO Architecture:** When a user attempts to log in, ArgoCD redirects them to Dex, which redirects to the configured identity provider. After successful authentication, Dex issues an OIDC token that ArgoCD uses to establish the user session. Dex serves as a federated OpenID Connect provider within the Kubernetes cluster.

**Prerequisites:** ArgoCD (v2.0+), Kubernetes cluster admin access, identity provider access (GitHub, Google, LDAP, etc.), and a domain name for ArgoCD with valid TLS certificates.

**Connector Configurations Provided (with full YAML examples):**
1. **GitHub OAuth** - Create OAuth app with callback URL (https://argocd.yourdomain.com/api/dex/callback), configure connector in argocd-cm ConfigMap with org/team restrictions, store client secret in argocd-secret using $variable syntax ($dex.github.clientSecret), and restart argocd-server/argocd-dex-server deployments.
2. **Google OIDC** - Create OAuth 2.0 Client ID in Google Cloud Console, use issuer https://accounts.google.com, with hostedDomains restriction for Google Workspace and scopes (openid, profile, email).
3. **LDAP** - Uses bind service account for searches, userSearch (baseDN, filter, username/idAttr/emailAttr/nameAttr attributes), and groupSearch configuration; supports ldaps:// and StartTLS. Secret stored as $dex.ldap.bindPW.
4. **SAML 2.0** - For enterprise IdPs (Okta, OneLogin, Azure AD), requires Entity ID, ACS URL, and Name ID format setup in the IdP; includes certificate and attribute mapping (usernameAttr, emailAttr, groupsAttr).

**Multiple Providers:** Dex supports configuring multiple connectors simultaneously (GitHub, Google, LDAP), presenting users with a provider choice during login.

**RBAC for SSO Users:** Configuration through argocd-rbac-cm ConfigMap maps identity provider groups to roles (admin, developer, qa) using policy.csv (g, subject, role format). Includes AppProject-level RBAC for restricting clusters/repositories per team.

**Troubleshooting:** Includes debug commands (kubectl logs for dex/server, configmap/secret checks, Dex health endpoint port-forward), verification via argocd CLI (get-user-info, can-i), and common mistakes (missing $ prefix in secrets, wrong callback URL, case-sensitive GitHub org names).

**Security Best Practices:** Always use TLS, restrict identity provider scope (specific orgs/domains/OUs), implement least-privilege RBAC, rotate secrets regularly, monitor authentication events with JSON logging.

A complete production-ready combined configuration example (GitHub + LDAP) is provided. The post concludes with key takeaways: Dex acts as identity broker, choose the right connector, configure RBAC carefully, monitor/troubleshoot with logs, and follow security best practices.

--- SOURCE 23: Overview - Argo CD - Declarative GitOps CD for Kubernetes ---
URL: https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/user-management

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Argo CD documentation page on User Management and Single Sign-On (SSO) configuration. It covers two main topics:

**Local Users/Accounts:**
- Argo CD has one built-in `admin` user with full system access; recommended for initial configuration only.
- Local users are defined in the `argocd-cm` ConfigMap using entries like `accounts.alice: apiKey, login` (each user can have apiKey and/or login capabilities).
- Maximum local account username length is 32 characters; users must have RBAC rules or fall back to `policy.default`.
- Users can be deleted by removing ConfigMap entries and password entries in `argocd-secret` via kubectl patch commands. The `admin` user can be disabled with `admin.enabled: "false"`.
- CLI commands available: `argocd account list`, `argocd account get`, `argocd account update-password`, and `argocd account generate-token`.
- Failed login rate limiting is controlled by environment variables: `ARGOCD_SESSION_FAILURE_MAX_FAIL_COUNT` (default 5), `ARGOCD_SESSION_FAILURE_WINDOW_SECONDS` (default 300 seconds), `ARGOCD_SESSION_MAX_CACHE_SIZE` (default 1000), and `ARGOCD_MAX_CONCURRENT_LOGIN_REQUESTS_COUNT` (default 50).

**SSO Configuration:**
- Two SSO options: bundled Dex OIDC provider (for providers not supporting OIDC like SAML/LDAP, or for Dex connector features) or an existing OIDC provider (Okta, OneLogin, Auth0, Microsoft, Keycloak, Google).
- **Dex**: Configured via `dex.config` in `argocd-cm`. Includes GitHub (OAuth2) and GitHub Enterprise examples, OIDC connector configuration, requesting additional ID token claims (via `scopes` and `insecureEnableGroups`), and retrieving claims via the UserInfo endpoint (`getUserInfo`).
- **Existing OIDC Provider**: Configured via `oidc.config` key with options including `allowedAudiences`, `skipAudienceCheckWhenTokenHasNoAudience` (defaults false for Argo CD ≥2.6.0), `requestedScopes`, `requestedIDTokenClaims`, `cliClientID`, `enablePKCEAuthentication`, and `logoutURL` for custom logout.
- **Token Revocation**: Argo CD implements server-side token revocation on logout for enhanced security; the `argocd logout` command degrades gracefully when the server is unreachable. Security best practices include short-lived tokens, enabling logout URLs, and monitoring token usage.
- **Custom root CA**: `rootCA` in `oidc.config` allows PEM-encoded custom certificates for verifying OIDC provider TLS.
- **Sensitive Data**: Values starting with `$` in configmaps are interpreted as secret references. Syntax `$<secret>:a.key.in.k8s.secret` references keys in Kubernetes secrets (default `argocd-secret`, or another named secret with the `app.kubernetes.io/part-of: argocd` label). Secret values must be base64 encoded once.
- **Certificate Verification**: Can be skipped via `oidc.tls.insecure.skip.verify: "true"` in `argocd-cm` for specific self-signed or invalid certificate scenarios.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The maximum length of a local account's username is 32.

This is a transcript of "GitOps Guide to the Galaxy (Ep 16): Using RBAC with ArgoCD," a Red Hat YouTube show hosted by Christian Hernandez and Chris Short, posted June 4, 2021. The episode covers how role-based access control (RBAC) works with Argo CD, particularly in the context of OpenShift and multi-tenant clusters.

Key topics covered:
- Argo CD is an open source, declarative, GitOps continuous delivery tool that automates deployment of services in Kubernetes environments.
- Core Argo CD concepts: An "Application" is a CRD representing a logical collection of manifests (could be simple like pod/service/route, or complex like full application deployments). An Argo CD "Project" is a logical grouping of applications used for multi-tenant isolation (team A can see project Foo, team B sees project Bar in the same Argo instance without knowing about each other).
- Argo CD has only two built-in roles: read-only and 100% admin (all or nothing). Any other roles must be custom-built.
- RBAC policies are written in a format: P (policy), role/user/group, resource (clusters, projects, applications, repositories), action (get, update, sync, create, delete), and specific target.
- Group mapping (G) connects groups from the authentication provider (e.g., OpenShift) to roles within Argo CD projects.
- Argo CD connects to authentication providers using OIDC. OpenShift does not support native OIDC connectors, so a bridge is needed.
- Dex was historically used as an OIDC bridge (lightweight and simple), but it is NOT officially supported with Red Hat GitOps operator. The bundled Dex OIDC provider is not supported; it is not on the roadmap (closed as "will not fix"), though Red Hat engineers do still work on Dex upstream.
- A live demo of configuring Dex with Argo CD failed due to a version compatibility bug (the wrong Dex tag/version being used), resulting in CrashLoopBackOff errors. This demonstrates the fragility of using the unsupported Dex route.
- The supported approach involves using the Red Hat SSO operator (RH-SSO/Keycloak). Steps include: installing the RH-SSO operator from OperatorHub, creating a namespace, deploying a Keycloak instance, creating an OIDC connector for Argo CD, creating a group claim so group membership passes through on login, then base64-encoding the generated token and loading it into Argo CD as a secret.
- Live troubleshooting during the show was performed using kubectl/oc commands (get pods, logs, watching crash loops).
- A question about how to handle OpenShift configs with Argo (how to set up the Git repo) was deferred to a future episode, described as "the $10 million question."
- The hosts announced they were taking a break for Red Hat Summit (returning around July 1), with an upcoming deeper Helm-focused episode featuring a Helm maintainer from Weaveworks (Scott).
- The hosts noted that documentation for Argo CD and Red Hat projects is lacking and encouraged viewers to contribute to documentation efforts as a way to break into open source.

The episode demonstration ultimately failed to fully complete due to the Dex version issue, but the hosts outlined both the unsupported (Dex) and supported (Red Hat SSO/Keycloak) approaches to integrating RBAC and SSO with Argo CD on OpenShift.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 25: Microsoft - Argo CD - Declarative GitOps CD for Kubernetes ---
URL: https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/user-management/microsoft

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a documentation guide from Argo CD's official documentation, covering how to configure Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) authentication for ArgoCD using various methods: OIDC with App Registration, SAML with Enterprise App using Dex, and App Registration using Dex.

**Entra ID App Registration Auth using OIDC:**
- Create a new App registration in Microsoft Entra ID with a redirect URI (Web platform, https://{argo-url}/auth/callback)
- Add a "Mobile and desktop applications" platform with redirect URI `http://localhost:8085/auth/callback` for ArgoCD CLI
- Credentials can be set up two ways: (a) Workload Identity Federation (recommended) - requires adding `azure.workload.identity/use: "true"` label to argocd-server pods, `azure.workload.identity/client-id` annotation to service account, and configuring federated credentials; or (b) Client Secret - create a new client secret in Certificates & secrets
- Setup permissions: grant `User.Read` permission under Microsoft Graph, and add groups claim via Token Configuration
- Associate users/groups via Enterprise applications
- Configure `argocd-cm` with `oidc.config` (including issuer `https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant_id}/v2.0`, clientID, and optional `azure.useWorkloadIdentity`), `argocd-secret` with client secret, and `argocd-rbac-cm` with RBAC policies mapping Azure group IDs to roles

**Azure AD Groups Overflow Resolution (200+ Groups):**
- Azure AD access tokens can contain a maximum of 200 groups; beyond that, overflow indicators (`_claim_names` and `_claim_sources`) are set instead of the `groups` claim
- Argo CD can auto-detect overflow and call the Microsoft Graph API to fetch the complete group list
- Requires `User.Read` delegated permission on the app registration
- Config includes `azure.enableUserGroupOverageClaim: true`, `graphApiEndpoint` (default `https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0`), and `userGroupOverageClaimCacheExpiration`
- Works by: detecting overflow indicators, checking User.Read scope, calling `POST /me/getMemberGroups` (up to 2048 groups, security-enabled only), caching resolved groups, and integrating into RBAC evaluation
- For sovereign clouds (Azure Government, China), override the graphApiEndpoint (e.g., `https://graph.microsoft.us/v1.0`)
- Warning: If Graph API is unavailable, users with 200+ groups cannot authenticate. Graph API failures cause 401 Unauthorized responses.

**Entra ID SAML Enterprise App Auth using Dex:**
- Create a Non-gallery Enterprise application with SAML configuration (Identifier/Reply URL: https://{url}/api/dex/callback, Sign on URL: https://{url}/auth/login)
- Configure claims: email (user.mail), group claim (Group ID source, "Group" name)
- Download SAML Signing Certificate (Base64 encode it), copy Login URL
- Configure `dex.config` in argocd-cm with type `saml`, including caData, ssoURL, entityIssuer, and attributes (usernameAttr: email, emailAttr: email, groupsAttr: Group)

**Entra ID App Registration Auth using Dex:**
- Use `dex.config` with type `microsoft` connector, including clientID, clientSecret, redirectURI (`http://localhost:8080/api/dex/callback`), tenant, and groups

**Validation:**
- Log in via ArgoCD UI using the "LOGIN VIA AZURE" button and verify group Object IDs in User Info
- Log in via CLI, which opens a browser for authorization code flow (redirect to `http://localhost:8085/auth/callback`), may show x509 certificate warnings for self-signed certs

**Domain hint (optional):**
- Set `domainHint` in `oidc.config` to add `domain_hint=` to the authorization request to Microsoft, reducing account discovery prompts in multi-tenant or federated environments. Default is empty (not sent).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Azure AD / Entra ID access tokens can contain a maximum of 200 groups. When a user belongs to more than 200 groups, Azure AD sets overflow indicators (`_claim_names` and `_claim_sources`) in the ID token instead of including the `groups` claim. This causes users to have no group-based RBAC permissions in Argo CD."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-26-argocd-google-gke-best-practices/view

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This OneUptime blog post (published Feb 26, 2026 by Nawaz Dhandala) provides a comprehensive guide to production best practices for running ArgoCD on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The article covers GKE-specific integration points including Autopilot vs Standard mode selection, Workload Identity configuration, private cluster setups, Google-managed certificates, internal load balancers, SSO with Google Workspace, multi-cluster management, monitoring with Google Cloud Managed Prometheus, node placement, and backup with GCS.

Key technical details covered:
- **GKE Autopilot vs Standard**: Autopilot is fully managed (like AWS Fargate), simpler but higher per-pod cost; Standard offers full node control and is more cost-effective at scale. GKE Standard recommended for most production setups.
- **Installation**: Uses Helm with HA configuration (2 controller replicas, autoscaling server/repoServer replicas, redis-ha enabled) with `helm install argocd argo/argo-cd -n argocd --create-namespace -f values-gke.yaml`.
- **Workload Identity**: Maps K8s service accounts to GCP service accounts (equivalent of AWS IRSA), eliminating key management. Requires annotating the service account with `iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account`.
- **Private clusters**: No special config needed if ArgoCD runs on the same cluster; remote private clusters require private endpoint connectivity via VPC peering, Cloud VPN, or Cloud Interconnect.
- **Certificates**: GKE Managed Certificates work with external Ingress but NOT with internal GKE Ingress (which requires regional pre-shared certs or Kubernetes TLS Secrets); Gateway API (gke-l7-rilb) recommended for newer clusters.
- **SSO**: Configure Google as OIDC provider, but note Google's standard OIDC flow does not include Google Groups membership for RBAC (requires Dex Google connector with Google Directory API).
- **Multi-cluster**: Use `argocd cluster add` and ApplicationSets with cluster generators for multi-cluster deployments.
- **Node placement**: Dedicated node pool with taints/tolerations and node selectors to pin ArgoCD.
- **Backup**: Daily CronJob backing up Applications and AppProjects YAML to GCS bucket for ArgoCD resources.

The article concludes that combining GKE's managed Kubernetes with ArgoCD's GitOps model yields a robust, secure, automated deployment platform, recommending HA installation, configuring Workload Identity from day one, and using internal load balancers. The post also promotes OneUptime for unified observability, alerting, and status pages. The page also contains extensive product navigation content for the OneUptime platform itself (monitoring, incident management, observability, logs, metrics, traces, Kubernetes/Docker monitoring, workflows, etc.).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Building a Fleet with ArgoCD and GKE | Google Cloud Blog ---
URL: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/containers-kubernetes/building-a-fleet-with-argocd-and-gke

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Google Cloud blog post (by Nick Eberts, Product Manager GKE, and Shannon Kularathna, Technical Writer GKE) demonstrates how to use ArgoCD and Argo Rollouts to automate the management (state) of a Fleet of GKE clusters. The tutorial covers three key journeys for cluster operators: (1) zero-touch onboarding of new GKE application clusters to a Fleet using labels, (2) deploying new applications that automatically inherit baseline multi-tenant configurations and RBAC policies, and (3) progressively rolling out application versions across groups (waves) of clusters with manual approval between waves.

**Architecture**: The post uses a hub-and-spoke architecture to preserve ArgoCD's UI/UX across a Fleet. A centralized GKE cluster hosts ArgoCD, and every application cluster is added as a Secret in the ArgoCD namespace with specific labels. ArgoCD's sync agent continuously watches config repositories and actuates changes across the Fleet based on cluster labels (e.g., `env: "multi-cluster-controller"` and `env: "prod"`). Underlying infrastructure (VPC, subnets, IP ranges) is set up using a Google-provided demo tool, and the control cluster is configured with Managed Anthos Service Mesh (ASM) and Multi Cluster Ingress (MCI).

**Key technologies**: Multi Cluster Ingress provides a single anycast IP in front of a global layer 7 load balancer that routes traffic to the closest GKE cluster, offering performance and regional failure resiliency. Managed Anthos Service Mesh handles pod-to-pod traffic across the Fleet with mTLS and automatic failover. Clusters can be added to ArgoCD via the `argocli add cluster` command (which inserts a bearer token with clusteradmin permissions) or via Connect Gateway and Fleet Workload Identity (which allow custom labels and Google OAuth2 token authentication). New clusters labeled `env=prod` automatically get baseline tooling like ASM Gateways. The demo code is available on GitHub (gke-poc-toolkit-demos).

**Progressive rollouts**: ArgoCD rollouts resemble Kubernetes Deployments with additional control fields. The demo uses a canary strategy with two 4-minute steps, where the rollout controller adjusts Istio virtual service weights to route 20% of traffic to the new image. Each step runs an analysis template using Prometheus to check success rates; if the success rate is 95% or greater, the rollout proceeds, otherwise it rolls back (setting traffic to 100% to stable pods). After all steps complete, the rollout labels the new deployment as stable and deletes the previous version. The demo covers promoting versions from a `wave-1` git branch to `wave-2`, and finally to `main` as the stable version.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"ArgoCD is a CNCF tool that provides GitOps continuous delivery for Kubernetes. ArgoCD's UX/UI is one of its most valuable features." "MCI is going to provide better performance to all traffic getting routing into your cluster from an external client by giving you a single anycast IP in front of a global layer 7 load balancer that routes traffic to the GKE cluster in your Fleet that is closest to your clients." "The rollout controller then adjusts the Istio virtual service weight so that 20% of traffic to that cluster is routed to Pods that use the new image." "If the success rate is 95% or greater, the rollout moves on to the next step. If the success rate is less than 95%, the rollout controller rolls the change back by setting the Istio virtual service weight to 100% for the Pods running the stable version of the image." "ArgoCD rollouts are similar to Kubernetes Deployments, with some additional fields to control the rollout."

<summary>
This page details the security architecture of Argo CD, a GitOps deployment tool. Key security topics covered include:

- **Authentication**: All API authentication uses JSON Web Tokens (JWTs). The local admin user exchanges credentials for a JWT via the /api/v1/session endpoint; these tokens have no expiration but are immediately revoked upon password change. SSO users authenticate via OAuth2/OIDC providers with tokens issued by the IDP. Automation tokens are project-scoped with configurable expiration and can be revoked.

- **Authorization**: RBAC is enforced by comparing JWT group claims against roles/rules in the policy.

- **TLS**: All inter-component communication uses TLS, with the option to enforce TLS 1.2 via the --tlsminversion flag.

- **Sensitive Information**: Argo CD redacts sensitive data in API payloads and logs. External cluster credentials are stored as Kubernetes Secrets. Procedures for rotating bearer tokens and revoking cluster access are provided.

- **Cluster RBAC**: Default cluster-admin privileges can be narrowed by modifying ClusterRoles. Resource exclusion is recommended for denying access to specific resource types.

- **Auditing**: Git commit history provides natural audit logging, supplemented by Kubernetes Events that track application activity and actor identity.

- **Webhook Payloads**: Webhook payloads are treated as untrusted and only used to trigger application refresh for reconciliation.
</summary>

URL: https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-26-scale-argocd-1000-applications/view

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This technical blog post (published Feb 26, 2026 by Nawaz Dhandala on OneUptime, an open-source observability platform) is a comprehensive guide on scaling ArgoCD to handle 1,000+ applications. At this scale, a single application controller hits its limits, requiring intentional architecture changes such as controller sharding, aggressive caching, repo server horizontal scaling, and careful Redis sizing.

The guide outlines the following key steps:
- **Step 1: Controller Sharding** - Distribute destination clusters across multiple controller instances (3 replicas recommended at 750-1000 apps, 4-5 for larger deployments), using StatefulSet ordinal index to determine shards. Note that sharding only helps when apps target multiple clusters.
- **Step 2: Scale Repo Server** - Use 5 replicas with a parallelism limit of 10 each, providing 50 concurrent manifest generation operations.
- **Step 3: Maximize Cache Efficiency** - Configure Redis HA (3 replicas, gzip compression), set cache expiration to 24 hours, and leverage repo server request deduplication (ArgoCD automatically deduplicates simultaneous same-repo requests).
- **Step 4: Optimize Reconciliation** - Increase reconciliation interval to 5 minutes with jitter, and rely on webhooks for near-instant detection of Git changes.
- **Step 5: Resource Exclusions** - Aggressively exclude noisy resources (Cilium identities, events, leases, EndpointSlices) and ignore differences for frequently changing fields.
- **Step 6: Dedicated Node Pools** - Plan for ~27 CPU and 40Gi RAM total across controller (3x3 CPU/4Gi), repo server (5x2 CPU/3Gi), server (2x1 CPU/512Mi), and Redis HA (3x2 CPU/4Gi); two to three 16 CPU/32GB dedicated nodes recommended.
- **Step 7: Repository Architecture** - Split monorepos by team/domain (~50-100 apps per repo), use credential templates, and enable shallow cloning for repos with large histories.
- **Step 8: Monitoring** - Set critical alerts for uneven cluster app distribution, reconciliation backlog, and repo server saturation.
- **Step 9: Disaster Recovery** - Export all applications, projects, and application sets; store backups in a separate Git repository managed independently of ArgoCD.

The article concludes that with sharded controllers (3+ replicas), 5 repo server replicas, Redis HA with compression, aggressive caching, monitoring, dedicated node pools, and disaster recovery planning, ArgoCD remains a reliable GitOps platform well beyond 1,000 applications. The post was technically validated on May 20, 2026.

URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yATHNHLWj-M

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a summary of Akuity's webinar titled "How to Best Scale and Optimize Argo CD for Kubernetes Deployments," the second session in Akuity's GitOps webinar series, presented by Christian Hernandez (Argo project maintainer and Head of Community at Akuity), posted 26 February 2025. The webinar provides practical implementation guidance for production-ready GitOps practices with Argo CD, covering installation, scaling, sharding, repository design, application syncing, ApplicationSets, and application dependency management.

Key topics covered:

1. **Installation Methods**: The webinar compares installation approaches—raw YAML, Helm charts, operators (maintained by Red Hat), and Infrastructure-as-Code (Terraform, Pulumi). Hernandez strongly recommends the Helm chart despite being a kustomize enthusiast, because the Argo CD Helm chart is officially supported and maintained by the Argo project community (with contributions from Intuit, Akuity, and Red Hat). He recommends using kustomize with the Helm plugin to combine both approaches.

2. **Scaling Argo CD**: The HA install provides scaling mechanisms, with three nodes recommended (Redis requires three nodes for quorum). The three main controllers to scale are the repository controller, API server, and application controller. Scaling the application controller automatically enables sharding. A Helm upgrade tip was shared: always use `--reuse-values` before applying new values because order matters. The repo server is typically the first component to show trouble, especially with monorepos (first indication to scale).

3. **Sharding**: Sharding assigns clusters to shards (each pod represents a single shard), is cluster-scoped (not application-specific), and three algorithms exist: Legacy (hash-based), Round Robin (uniform but resource-intensive with frequent cluster changes), and Consistent Hashing (currently alpha). Clusters can be manually assigned/pinned to specific shards (e.g., separate shards for dev, test, and production environments). Recommended baseline scaling values were shared from Red Hat.

4. **Repository Structure**: Poly-repo approach recommended with a control plane repo (for corporate standard builds, Argo CD installation, secrets managers) and separate application-specific repositories (one repo for all tenants, or per-tenant repos). Intuit uses three repos including a separate cluster add-ons repo. Separation helps performance since one repo server process handles sync/refresh operations. Best practice is having Argo CD manage itself (GitOps-ing the values file, storing configs in git).

5. **Application Syncing**: Two customization options—application-specific sync options (global settings) and resource-specific annotations. Recommended sync options include `createNamespace=true` (debated by Hernandez and Red Hat's Gerald) and `applyOutOfSyncOnly=true`. Resource-specific annotations include `prune=false`, `delete=false`, and `replace=true` (used for jobs that need to re-run).

6. **ApplicationSets**: ApplicationSets are "application factories" that solve the one-to-one limitation of Applications (single destination). They use generators (list, git repo, pull request, etc.) and native templating. ApplicationSets are dynamic and don't replace App of Apps—both are used as part of larger fleet deployments.

7. **Application Dependencies**: Three main approaches—eventual consistency, App of Apps patterns, and Progressive syncs in ApplicationSets. Prerequisites include setting up readiness/liveness probes (Argo CD considers apps healthy without them immediately), writing Lua health checks for custom CRDs, and enabling the Argo CD application resource health check (disabled by default per issue #3781, which the author disagrees with). The `skipDryRunOnMissingResource` sync option helps with eventual consistency, avoiding dry-run failures before CRDs exist.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 14: Overview - Argo CD - Declarative GitOps CD for Kubernetes ---
URL: https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/high_availability

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the Argo CD documentation on High Availability and Performance Optimization. It covers how to run Argo CD in a highly available manner and provides extensive scaling and tuning guidance for the main components.

**High Availability Overview:** Argo CD is largely stateless; all data persists as Kubernetes objects in etcd. Redis is a disposable cache that can be rebuilt without service disruption. HA manifests are provided, running more containers with Redis in HA mode. The HA installation requires at least three different nodes due to pod anti-affinity rules, and IPv6-only clusters are not supported.

**argocd-repo-server settings:**
- `--parallelismlimit` flag controls concurrent manifest generations to avoid OOM kills
- Clones repos into `/tmp` (or `TMPDIR`); mount a persistent volume to avoid disk exhaustion with many repos
- `ARGOCD_GIT_ATTEMPTS_COUNT` retries failed `git ls-remote` operations (used for resolving ambiguous revisions like HEAD)
- `--repo-cache-expiration` (default 24h) controls manifest cache; `1h` suggested for low-volume environments (helps with Kustomize remote bases or Helm chart changes without version bumps)
- `ARGOCD_EXEC_TIMEOUT` (default 90s) controls config management tool execution timeout; `SIGTERM` is issued, then `SIGKILL` after `ARGOCD_EXEC_FATAL_TIMEOUT`
- CMP `discovery` option copies repos into separate directories per plugin, placing heavy load on disk; consider disabling or using plugin tar stream exclusions
- Metrics: `argocd_git_request_total` (tags: repo, request_type: ls-remote/fetch); `ARGOCD_ENABLE_GRPC_TIME_HISTOGRAM` for RPC performance (expensive to query and store)

**argocd-application-controller settings:**
- Two queues: app reconciliation (ms) and app syncing (seconds), controlled by `--status-processors` (default 20) and `--operation-processors` (default 10). For 1000 applications, use 50 and 25 respectively
- `--hydration-processors` (default 5) controls Source Hydrator queue; keyed by source repo, target revision, destination branch
- Manifest generation is the most time-consuming part; `Context deadline exceeded` errors can be addressed with `--repo-server-timeout-seconds` and scaling up repo-server
- Controller caches only preferred resource versions; `kubectl convert` failures fall back to slower Kubernetes API queries
- Polls Git every 3m by default; configurable via `timeout.reconciliation` and `timeout.reconciliation.jitter` in `argocd-cm` ConfigMap
- Cluster sharding: increase StatefulSet replicas plus `ARGOCD_CONTROLLER_REPLICAS` env var; `--sharding-method` supports `legacy`, `uid`, `round-robin`, `consistent-hashing` (the latter two are experimental alpha features)
- Per-cluster shard assignment via `shard` field in cluster secret
- `ARGOCD_ENABLE_GRPC_TIME_HISTOGRAM`, `ARGOCD_CLUSTER_CACHE_LIST_PAGE_BUFFER_SIZE`, `ARGOCD_CLUSTER_CACHE_BATCH_EVENTS_PROCESSING` (default true), `ARGOCD_CLUSTER_CACHE_EVENTS_PROCESSING_INTERVAL` (default 100ms), `ARGOCD_APPLICATION_TREE_SHARD_SIZE` (splits application tree across Redis keys to reduce traffic)
- Metrics: `argocd_app_reconcile`, `argocd_app_k8s_request_total`

**argocd-server:** Stateless and least likely to cause issues; scale to 3+ replicas with `ARGOCD_API_SERVER_REPLICAS`. `ARGOCD_GRPC_MAX_SIZE_MB` (default 200MB; may need increase for 3000+ apps). `server.glob.cache.size` (default 10000) caches compiled glob patterns for RBAC policy evaluation.

**argocd-dex-server and argocd-redis:** DEX uses in-memory DB (inconsistent across instances); Redis is pre-configured for only three total servers/sentinels.

**Monorepo Scaling Considerations:** Repo server keeps one local clone; if manifest generation changes local files, only one concurrent generation per instance is allowed, significantly slowing monorepos with 50+ apps.

1. **Fully qualified Git references:** Using `refs/heads/main`, `refs/tags/v1.0.0`, `refs/pull/123/head`, `refs/merge-requests/123/head` instead of short names significantly improves repo-server performance in large monorepos by optimizing ref resolution and caching.

2. **Concurrent processing:** Parallel processing works when generation has no side effects. Helm apps to same directory now generate in parallel by default (since v3.0). Custom plugins: avoid temp files and add `.argocd-allow-concurrency` file or use sidecar plugin. No workaround for Kustomize parameter overrides.

3. **Manifest Paths Annotation:** `argocd.argoproj.io/manifest-generate-paths` annotation (working since v2.11 without webhooks) limits cache invalidation to specified semicolon-separated paths. If no modified files match, cache stays valid and reconciliation is skipped. Supported for webhooks only with GitHub, GitLab, Gogs. Skipped for shallow clones (depth > 0). When used, only annotation-specified resources are sent to CMP. Efficiency measured via `argocd_webhook_requests_total` and `argocd_webhook_store_cache_attempts_total` (high `successful=true` ratio indicates good performance). Cache warming can be disabled per-repo (`webhookManifestCacheWarmDisabled: true` via `argocd repo edit --webhook-manifest-cache-warm-disabled`) or globally (`ARGOCD_WEBHOOK_MANIFEST_CACHE_WARM_DISABLED=true`), recommended for large monorepos with plain YAML.

4. **Sync timeout jitter:** `ARGOCD_RECONCILIATION_JITTER` spreads out periodic refreshes. Webhook refresh jitter via `webhook.refresh.jitter` and `webhook.refresh.jitter.threshold` in `argocd-cm`; worker count via `server.webhook.refresh.workers` (default 20).

Final backoff = `max(globalBackoff, perItemBackoff)`.

--- SOURCE 15: [Ep.16] Tuning OpenShift GitOps for performance at scale :: TechBlog about OpenShift/Ansible/Satellite and much more ---
URL: https://blog.stderr.at/gitopscollection/2026-03-27-openshift-gitops-performance-tuning

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (Ep.16 of a GitOps blog series) by Thomas Jungbauer, published April 15, 2026, is a comprehensive guide to performance tuning for OpenShift GitOps / Argo CD at scale. Argo CD tends to slow down as clusters, applications, and repositories grow, causing longer refreshes, sluggish UI, and frustrating experiences.

The article first explains Argo CD's core components in data-flow order: Repo Server (connects to Git, generates manifests, uses Redis for caching), Redis (caches rendered manifests, default 24h TTL), Server (API/UI), ApplicationSet Controller (reconciles ApplicationSets), and Application Controller (reconciles desired vs. live state).

Key tuning settings covered:

**Repo Server optimizations:**
- **Git shallow cloning (depth):** By default Argo CD clones full repo history; setting `depth` (e.g., 1) in the repository Secret drastically reduces fetch time (~half). Example showed fetch time dropping from ~1011ms to ~559ms.
- **ARGOCD_REPO_SERVER_PARALLELISM_LIMIT (Default 0/unlimited):** Bounds concurrent Git fetches/manifest generation to prevent OOM kills during burst activity. Recommended start: 20.
- **ARGOCD_GIT_LS_REMOTE_PARALLELISM_LIMIT (Default 0):** Protects the Git provider from being overwhelmed by concurrent `git ls-remote` checks; prevents rate limiting and applications stuck in "Unknown" state. Recommended: 20.
- **ARGOCD_EXEC_TIMEOUT (Default 90s):** Max time for child processes (Helm, Kustomize, plugins) to render manifests; raise to 180s+ for heavy charts.
- **ARGOCD_EXEC_FATAL_TIMEOUT (Default 10s):** Hard kill deadline after SIGTERM; author recommends leaving at default.
- **ARGOCD_GIT_ATTEMPTS_COUNT (Default 1):** Retry count for failed Git operations; recommended 3-5 on flaky networks.
- **ARGOCD_REPO_CACHE_EXPIRATION (Default 24h):** Redis cache TTL; keep at 24h, do not lower it to catch floating tags quickly as it degrades performance.
- **ARGOCD_REVISION_CACHE_LOCK_TIMEOUT (Default 10s):** TTL to deduplicate concurrent rendering of the same commit, preventing cache stampedes; raise for large charts.
- **ARGOCD_SERVER_REPO_SERVER_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (Default 60):** How long the API server waits for repo server responses (avoids "context deadline exceeded" in UI); align with ARGOCD_EXEC_TIMEOUT.

**Application Controller:**
- **Sharding:** Horizontally scales the controller across multiple replicas; each replica reconciles only applications whose destination clusters map to its shard. Algorithms: `legacy` (stable hash, can be unbalanced), `round-robin` (more even, often better default), `consistent-hashing` (may improve balance but not officially documented in OpenShift GitOps). Only useful with more than one cluster.
- **timeout.reconciliation (Default 3m):** Polling interval for comparing desired vs. live state; increase to 600s-3600s with Git webhooks to drastically reduce baseline load.
- **timeout.reconciliation.jitter (Default 60s):** Random delay to prevent applications from polling in synchronized spikes; keep non-zero.
- **controller.status.processors (Default 20):** Concurrent status comparisons; raise to 50-100 at large scale.
- **controller.operation.processors (Default 10):** Concurrent sync operations; raise when sync queue backs up.
- **ARGOCD_APPLICATION_CONTROLLER_REPO_SERVER_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (Default 60):** Controller→repo-server gRPC deadline; raise to 120-300s for slow manifest RPCs. Must be set under spec.controller.env, not spec.extraConfig.
- **ARGOCD_APPLICATION_CONTROLLER_KUBECTL_PARALLELISM_LIMIT (Default 20):** Max concurrent kubectl child processes; should match or sit slightly below operation processors (e.g., 50).

The article provides a comparison table of all settings with defaults, recommended values, and OpenShift GitOps (ArgoCD CR) configuration snippets. It emphasizes that tuning should be evidence-led and done in order of leverage: first reduce unnecessary Git/render work (shallow clones, cache TTLs, webhooks), then align timeouts, then bound concurrency, and finally scale out with sharding and replicas.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"OpenShift GitOps performance is rarely fixed by a single knob. The repo server, application controller, API server, Redis, and your Git provider all interact: a slow manifest render stresses the repo server; an aggressive client timeout fails the UI even when rendering would succeed; unbounded parallelism can OOM the repo server; tight kubectl concurrency can leave sync operations queued on an otherwise healthy controller."

"A practical approach is to work in order of leverage: reduce unnecessary Git and render work (for example shallow clones, cache TTLs, and webhooks so you are not polling blindly), then align related timeouts (ARGOCD_EXEC_TIMEOUT, controller and API server deadlines to the repo server), then bound concurrency (repo-server parallelism, Git ls-remote limits, status and operation processors, kubectl parallelism) before you scale out with sharding and replicas."

"Finally, treat tuning as evidence-led: change one major setting at a time, watch controller and repo-server memory, reconcile duration, API rates, and Git rate limits. What works for a small instance will not automatically transfer to thousands of applications or many managed clusters."

"There is no one-size-fits-all value here. The best approach is to start with a modest number such as 20 and monitor the behaviour of the repo server."

"In combination with Git webhooks, this setting [timeout.reconciliation] is one of the most important performance tweaks you can apply."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: HIPAA CI/CD Pipeline on AWS, GCP + Azure: 2026 Guide ---
URL: https://stonebridgetechsolutions.com/blog/hipaa-cicd-implementation-guide

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive implementation guide (published May 13, 2026) on building HIPAA-compliant CI/CD pipelines, authored by Lucas Jones, Founder of Stonebridge Tech Solutions. The guide focuses on architectural decisions rather than just listing compliance controls.

**Key HIPAA Controls Touching Pipelines:**
- § 164.308(a)(5)(ii)(C) Log-in monitoring (attributable deployments)
- § 164.308(a)(8) Periodic evaluation (security scans on every change)
- § 164.312(b) Audit controls (recorded, queryable deployments)
- § 164.312(c)(1) Integrity controls (signed artifacts, verified signatures)
- § 164.312(e)(1) Transmission security (encrypted, mutually-authenticated deploys)

**Three Core Architectural Decisions:**

1. **Parent/Child Pipeline Separation:** A parent pipeline (under 40 lines) owns compliance gates, approvals, evidence aggregation, and deployment authorization. Child pipelines own build/test/scan/package tasks. This prevents monolithic 1,500-line pipeline files that fail audit.

2. **Isolated Runners Per Environment:** Dedicated runners per environment with scoped IAM, signed/version-pinned runner images, and HIPAA-aligned infrastructure. Shared runners with broad IAM are the most common audit finding.

3. **Security Scanners as Policy Gates:** Scanners produce structured evidence (JSON/SARIF) fed into a policy engine (OPA/Rego) that blocks deployments if thresholds aren't met. Scanners running as "advisory" (deploy proceeds regardless) fails audit.

**Reference Architecture:** Six-stage pipeline with evidence flowing in one direction only. Evidence is written to immutable buckets (S3 Object Lock or GCS Bucket Lock) with write-once semantics. The policy gate evaluates the full evidence bundle before any deploy proceeds.

**GCP Implementation:** Uses GCS with Bucket Lock, Cloud KMS (HSM-backed keys), GKE with environment-specific node pools, Workload Identity, Artifact Registry, VPC-SC perimeters, and Identity-Aware Proxy.

**AWS Implementation:** Uses S3 with Object Lock (Compliance Mode), AWS KMS with CMKs, EKS with IRSA, ECR with immutable tags, Transit Gateway, and GovCloud variant for FedRAMP.

**Tooling Recommendations:** Buildah/Kaniko (build), Semgrep/CodeQL (SAST), Trivy (container scanning), tfsec+Checkov (IaC), Gitleaks (secrets), Cosign (signing), OPA/Rego (policy gates), S3/GCS Bucket Lock (evidence storage).

**Platform Preference:** GitLab CI/CD + Argo CD is the opinionated default for new HIPAA pipelines. GitHub Actions is workable but more constrained. Jenkins is not recommended.

**Common Mistakes:** Single thousand-line pipeline files, shared runners with broad IAM, advisory-only scanners, audit evidence stored in Git repos, and manual approval as the only control.

The guide concludes that "audit-ready" is a property of how the pipeline operates, not a state to achieve. An architecturally correct pipeline passes audits even when the auditor, team, and code change.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post from Harness (published October 7, 2024) provides an overview of software deployment strategies, covering six main approaches:

1. **Basic Deployment** – All nodes updated simultaneously with a new version. Simple, fast, and cheap, but the riskiest strategy with no outage protection and difficult rollbacks.

2. **Multi-Service Deployment** – All nodes updated with multiple new services simultaneously. Used when services have version dependencies. Simple and less risky than basic, but slow to roll back and not outage-proof.

3. **Rolling Deployment** – Nodes incrementally updated in batches. Relatively simple rollback and less risky than basic, but requires supporting both old and new versions simultaneously and is slower due to verification at each step.

4. **Blue-Green Deployment** – Two identical environments (blue/staging and green/production). Traffic is shifted from green to blue after testing. Simple, fast, and easy to rollback (flip traffic back), but costly due to environment replication and risk of wide-scale impact before rollback.

5. **Canary Deployment** – Incrementally releases to a subset of users (e.g., 2%, 25%, 75%, 100%). Lowest risk strategy, allows testing in production with real users, cheaper than blue-green, and fast/safe rollback. However, scripting can be complex and requires monitoring/instrumentation.

6. **A/B Testing** – Different versions run simultaneously as experiments using feature flags or routing rules. Focused on experimentation rather than deployment. Standard, easy, and cheap, but can break user experience and scripting can be complex.

The post recommends blue-green or canary deployments for mission-critical web applications. It cites a case study from Burst SMS where blue-green deployments reduced outage recovery from two hours to under five minutes (96% improvement). The article also discusses Continuous Verification (CV) for automated deployment verification and 24/7 service monitoring, and promotes Harness's continuous delivery tools for automating these strategies.
</summary>

Google Cloud announced at KubeCon that it successfully ran a **130,000-node Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster in experimental mode** — double the previously supported 65,000-node limit. 2. **Phase 2:** Introduced 65,000 low-priority batch Pods, then 104,000 medium-priority fine-tuning Pods (preempting 60% of batch workloads). Kueue preempted 39,000 Pods in 93 seconds with ~745 Pods/s churn.
3. **Phase 3:** Added 26,000 high-priority inference Pods, scaled to 52,000 Pods (40% capacity), preempting lower-priority jobs.
4. **Phase 4:** Scaled down inference by 50%, demonstrating elasticity and resource recovery.

Control plane remained stable: API server latencies stayed below thresholds, P99 Pod startup latency for inference was ~10 seconds, and throughput reached 1,000 operations/second for both Pod creation and binding. The authors note that demand for mega-clusters (20-65K nodes) is growing, and they anticipate stabilization around 100K nodes, with future needs requiring multi-cluster solutions like MultiKueue and managed DRANET for RDMA networking.

--- SOURCE 1: Authorization (RBAC) - Spinnaker ---
URL: https://spinnaker.io/docs/setup/other_config/security/authorization

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page documents Spinnaker's authorization (RBAC) capabilities, which are handled by the Fiat microservice (disabled by default). Fiat provides pluggable authorization mechanisms that allow restricting access to specific accounts and applications, running pipelines via automated triggers against access-controlled resources, and updating user roles from backing role providers.

Key concepts and important notes:
- Permissions are attached to applications and provider accounts, associating a role with READ, WRITE, or EXECUTE (apps only) options.
- Fiat's authorization model is an approve list that is open by default—resources that don't define access are considered unrestricted.
- Every permission is granted to a role; individual users cannot be granted permissions directly. Super admin access is also granted to roles.
- Account and application access control relationship: accounts can contain multiple applications, and applications can span multiple accounts. Access to one doesn't automatically grant access to the other.

Requirements: Authentication setup in Gate; an external role provider (Google Groups via G Suite, GitHub Organization, LDAP, SAML IdP, or OAuth2 with groups in claims); Fiat enabled in spinnaker.yml.

Implementation details:
- Accounts: Fiat queries Clouddriver for accounts. Two access types exist: READ and WRITE. Users need READ to view resources and WRITE to modify them. READ permissions are NOT implicitly granted by WRITE permissions (highly recommended to always add READ to any WRITE access).
- Applications: Three permission levels (EXECUTE, READ, WRITE). By default, READ also grants EXECUTE. This can be changed via the executeFallback property in fiat-local.yml to only grant WRITE users implicit EXECUTE.
- Example permission requirements: deleting a load balancer in account Z requires WRITE on the account; updating a pipeline requires WRITE on the app; running a pipeline requires just EXECUTE; running a pipeline in app X deploying to account Y requires EXECUTE on app X and WRITE on account Y.

Role providers include: YAML file (user↔role mapping), GitHub Teams, Google Groups, LDAP, and SAML Groups (which bring external roles).

Automated pipeline triggers require sufficient permissions, configured either via Pipeline Permissions (automatic creation of service accounts on demand) or Fiat service accounts.

The page also links to deeper reference documentation and sub-pages for Google Groups, LDAP, Pipeline Permissions, SAML, Service Accounts, and GitHub Teams authorization. Last modified April 17, 2026.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Fiat (Fix it Again Travis) is the authorization (authz) microservice of Spinnaker. It can grant access to users to execute pipelines, view infrastructure, etc. It is disabled by default."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Leveraging Role-based Access Control to secure Spinnaker CD ---
URL: https://www.opsmx.com/blog/how-to-implement-role-based-access-control-rbac-in-spinnaker-for-secure-delivery

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This OpsMx blog post (published by Ayan Ganguly, originally May 25, 2023, updated December 26, 2025) provides a guide to implementing Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) in Spinnaker for secure CI/CD delivery. The article explains that RBAC creates guardrails by restricting system access, helping with separation of duties, improved security, compliance, reduced risk, cost reduction, visibility into user actions, and audit readiness.

Key steps outlined for implementing RBAC in Spinnaker include:
1. **Identify users and define roles**: Spinnaker has built-in roles (ADMIN, READ_ONLY, OPERATOR, DEPLOY, READ_WRITE), and custom roles can be created via YAML files, GitHub teams, Google groups, LDAP, or SAML groups. Permissions control actions like creating applications, deploying pipelines, and managing infrastructure.
2. **Configure Spinnaker user accounts**: Integrate with an identity provider (IdP) such as Okta, Google Identity Platform, Azure Active Directory, or Auth0. Configuration files include gate.yml, clouddriver.yml, or spinnaker-local.yml.
3. **Define permissions**: For Spinnaker 1.21 and above, the built-in RBAC system "Fiat" is used. Versions prior to 1.21 require Kubernetes RBAC or custom authorization providers.
4. **Test and validate** the permissions manually.
5. **Regularly review and update** roles and permissions as organizational needs evolve.

The article also promotes **OpsMx ISD for Spinnaker**, which provides addons to secure user access to data, pipelines, infrastructure, and deployments. It enables management of user groups, user roles, feature visibility guardrails (feature flags), cloud/target destination permissions, and DevOps tool chain permissions (e.g., Jenkins). OpsMx claims these tools enable audit-readiness and can accelerate software release velocity and deployment speed by 10x. The post includes links to related content on SAML authentication (with JumpCloud and Okta) and configuring groups with restricted cloud permissions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
RBAC ensures authorized and intended access to the resources to avoid risks and enhance security. In short RBAC helps enterprises with: Improved security, Compliance, Decreased security risk and breaches around sensitive data, Reduced cost, Complete visibility into who’s doing what, Enabling audit readiness.

--- SOURCE 3: RBAC In Spinnaker - Groups, Application vs. Account Permissions and How to Use Them - Jason McIntosh ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jMR1zQOfhs0

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a presentation by Jason McIntosh of Armory, Inc. on Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) in Spinnaker, delivered to the Continuous Delivery Foundation (viewed 384 times, posted 4 Nov 2022). The presentation examines two distinct types of permissions in Spinnaker: account permissions and application permissions.

AUTHORIZATION/ARCHITECTURE: Spinnaker is built on Spring Security and supports OAuth 2, SAML, LDAP, basic form, and X509 authentication. Authentication is handled at Gate (the entry point) using internal headers (e.g., X-Spinnaker-User, X-Spinnaker-Groups). Authorization is handled independently at a service called Fiat, which syncs information and generates a cache of authentication/authorization data. A key principle: Spinnaker doesn't care about individual usernames—all assignments are done via GROUPS. Group info can come from login assertions (SAML, OIDC), G Suite, or LDAP. Identity providers typically limit groups to 100-150 per login (Okta ~100, Microsoft/OAuth2 ~150); LDAP has no such limit but has scaling issues. Gate can merge internal and external groups into a cached identity.

ACCOUNT PERMISSIONS: Accounts are the target deployment environments (AWS, GCP, K8s clusters). They support READ and WRITE permissions only, defined in configuration at account creation. Key caution: WRITE does NOT extend READ (which causes problems); also, Spinnaker's account permissions have NO correlation to the permissions Spinnaker has in the target cloud—Spinnaker abstracts cloud provider authentication away. Limiting Spinnaker to a namespace/region in config doesn't prevent deployments to other namespaces/regions (results are simply not visible in the UI, and pipelines may fail because Spinnaker won't cache non-configured remote resources). Users should scope the service account/assume-role permissions appropriately to avoid security holes.

APPLICATION PERMISSIONS: Applications are abstractions around pipelines and can have permissions changed on the fly (via UI or config). They support READ, WRITE, and EXECUTE permissions. Create permission (restricting who can create new applications) is config-file only, and combined with regex allows patterns like "only team X can create prod apps." Changing app permissions triggers a background sync to Fiat that can be expensive (seconds in small orgs, up to 50 seconds in large ones). Pipelines run with the permissions of whoever runs/triggers them.

AUTOMATED TRIGGERS: For automated triggers (Docker, GitHub), Spinnarker uses internal service accounts (abstractions around authorization containing only roles, no authentication). Two methods: old-style service account permissions (still default) and newer, easier "pipeline permissions" which dynamically generate a service account via a roles block, though it requires sync completion before editing.

KEY LIMITATIONS/CAUTIONS:
- You cannot set permissions on a group unless you're already a member of all those groups (prevents privilege escalation).
- Artifacts/resources (e.g., GitHub repos, API fetches) have NO permissions set, so anyone could access sensitive repos used in configurations—an unresolved issue.
- Automated triggers must have EXECUTE permissions on the application or they fail silently with no error.
- Users must have READ permissions or pipelines will time out/fail.
- Manual Judgement stages can propagate/elevate permissions—the pipeline's permissions change to whoever approves the stage, enabling patterns like "everyone triggers, but only change control group deploys to prod."
- If authorization isn't enabled, the permissions combo box won't appear; these features have existed since at least Spinnaker 1.22.

The presentation also covered troubleshooting via the /auth/user endpoint on Gate, the authorities block (roles vs. groups), improvements in Fiat sync performance, and resources on GitHub (including running Spinnaker locally with a dev Okta instance), Spinnaker.io docs (including an X509 walkthrough with OpenSSL commands), and an Armory permissions matrix.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Individual user information doesn't mean anything to Spinnaker... what it cares about is [the user] is a member of groups... all assignments are done via groups.", "Write does not extend read... you can grant something right permissions without granting it read permissions. I do not recommend that that causes some very goofy behavior in some of the systems.", "Just because you limit a resource in Spinnaker does not mean that you're limited in the Target account.", "Pipelines will run with the permissions of who runs it... the caller of a pipeline is the one that is going to run with the permissions and it's the callers groups that are associated with it.", "You won't be able to set any permissions unless you're also a member of all the groups that your permissions are... that would be a privilege escalation. Spinnaker will not let that happen."
</key_excerpts>
