**3. Security Integration**

*RBAC model (Fiat)*

- Official Spinnaker docs: "Fiat (Fix it Again Travis) is the authorization (authz) microservice of Spinnaker. It can grant access to users to execute pipelines, view infrastructure, etc. It is disabled by default." Permissions attach to applications and provider accounts, associating a role with READ, WRITE, or EXECUTE (apps only). "Fiat's authorization model is an approve list that is open by default — resources that don't define access are considered unrestricted." Every permission is granted to a role; individual users cannot be granted permissions directly; super admin access is granted to roles. Access to an account doesn't automatically grant access to an application in it or vice versa. Requirements: authentication setup in Gate; an external role provider (Google Groups via G Suite, GitHub Organization, LDAP, SAML IdP, or OAuth2 with groups in claims); Fiat enabled in spinnaker.yml. Account permissions: READ and WRITE types; "READ permissions are NOT implicitly granted by WRITE permissions (highly recommended to always add READ to any WRITE access)." Application permissions: EXECUTE, READ, WRITE; by default READ also grants EXECUTE (changeable via the `executeFallback` property in fiat-local.yml). Example: deleting a load balancer in account Z requires WRITE on account; updating a pipeline requires WRITE on app; running a pipeline requires just EXECUTE; running a pipeline in app X deploying to account Y requires EXECUTE on app X and WRITE on account Y. Role providers: YAML file (user↔role mapping), GitHub Teams, Google Groups, LDAP, SAML Groups. Automated pipeline triggers require sufficient permissions via Pipeline Permissions (automatic service-account creation on demand) or Fiat service accounts. (Last modified April 17, 2026) [24]

- OpsMx RBAC guide: RBAC helps with "Improved security, Compliance, Decreased security risk and breaches around sensitive data, Reduced cost, Complete visibility into who's doing what, Enabling audit readiness." Built-in roles: ADMIN, READ_ONLY, OPERATOR, DEPLOY, READ_WRITE; custom roles via YAML files, GitHub teams, Google groups, LDAP, or SAML groups. Integrate an IdP such as Okta, Google Identity Platform, Azure Active Directory, or Auth0; configuration files include gate.yml, clouddriver.yml, or spinnaker-local.yml. Fiat is the built-in RBAC system "for Spinnaker 1.21 and above"; versions prior to 1.21 require Kubernetes RBAC or custom authorization providers. Test/validate permissions; review roles regularly. OpsMx ISD addons add user-group/role management, feature visibility guardrails (feature flags), cloud/target destination permissions, DevOps tool-chain permissions (e.g., Jenkins). (Updated December 26, 2025) [25]

- Jason McIntosh's CDF talk ("RBAC In Spinnaker - Groups, Application vs. Account Permissions") details that Spinnaker is built on Spring Security and supports "OAuth 2, SAML, LDAP, basic form, and X509 authentication." Authentication is handled at Gate using internal headers (X-Spinnaker-User, X-Spinnaker-Groups); authorization is handled independently at Fiat, which syncs information and generates a cache. "Individual user information doesn't mean anything to Spinnaker... all assignments are done via groups." Group info can come from login assertions (SAML, OIDC), G Suite, or LDAP; identity providers typically limit groups to 100–150 per login (Okta ~100, Microsoft/OAuth2 ~150); LDAP has no limit but has scaling issues; Gate can merge internal and external groups. Accounts support READ/WRITE only; "Write does not extend read... that causes some very goofy behavior" — always grant both. Account permissions have NO correlation to the permissions Spinnaker has in the target cloud; limiting Spinnaker to a namespace/region in config does NOT prevent deployments elsewhere, so scope the service account/assume-role permissions. Applications support READ/WRITE/EXECUTE; create permission is config-file only, and combined with regex allows patterns like "only team X can create prod apps." Changing app permissions triggers a background Fiat sync that can take up to 50 seconds in large orgs. "Pipelines will run with the permissions of whoever runs it." Automated triggers use internal service accounts; newer "pipeline permissions" dynamically generate a service account via a roles block but require sync completion before editing. Key limitations: you cannot set permissions on a group unless you're already a member of all those groups ("that would be a privilege escalation. Spinnaker will not let that happen"); artifacts/resources (GitHub repos, API fetches) have NO permissions (an unresolved issue); automated triggers must have EXECUTE or fail silently; users must have READ or pipelines time out; Manual Judgement stages can propagate/elevate permissions (the pipeline's permissions change to whoever approves), enabling patterns like "everyone triggers, but only change control group deploys to prod." Troubleshoot via the /auth/user endpoint on Gate. (Posted Nov 4, 2022; features existed since at least Spinnaker 1.22.) [26]

- Armory docs on Fiat permissions: "By default, it is not enabled, so users are able to perform any action in Spinnaker. When Fiat is enabled, users start with no permissions and must be explicitly granted permissions." Roles are maintained in an external identity provider and are case-insensitive. For AWS, a role needs both READ and WRITE on a Clouddriver account to deploy an AMI. Front50 permissions are controlled via service accounts created through cURL commands; all trigger-configured pipelines must have "Run as" permission or they fail; Armory recommends one service account per role/group to prevent privilege escalation. Example roles: fiat-admin (superuser), admin, dev, qa, ops. Verification: GET `$GATE_URL/applications`, GET `$GATE_URL/credentials`, `curl -s $FRONT50/serviceAccounts`, `curl -s $FIAT/authorize/$user-or-service-account`. Limitations: "Fiat does not support Pub Sub triggers or authenticating webhooks with group permissions." (Last modified October 17, 2023) [27]

*Authentication via OAuth/SAML/LDAP*

- Covered above: Spring Security with OAuth 2, SAML, LDAP, basic form, X509; Gate + Fiat; IdP integrations (Okta, Google Identity Platform, Azure AD, Auth0); Google Groups, GitHub Teams, LDAP, SAML groups as role providers. [24][25][26][27]
- The Spinnaker Basics 2026 workshop: change the default admin password; use SAML or OAuth2 in production. [13]
- The Spinnaker-on-GCP guide enables GSuite account login to restrict access to organization members, with the caveat that the default load balancer health check path is `/` but should be changed to `/health`. [28]

*Secrets management (Vault, GCP Secret Manager, Kubernetes Secrets)*

- Harness/Armory best practice: "Application secrets should not be passed through Spinnaker or any other deployment tool as this is not safe from a security standpoint. If the tool is breached you now have all applications secrets that were passed through the pipeline exposed. The only things that should ever be passed through a deployment tool are location and/or references to the secret." The application should fetch the secret itself during startup — for VMs at bootstrap; for Kubernetes via init-container, sidecar, or both. References: HashiCorp sidecar approach, Banzai Cloud, dynamic Vault agent sidecar tutorial; GoDaddy kubernetes-external-secrets for AWS Secrets Manager + Vault. [29]

- Spinnaker's external configuration (Spring Cloud Config) manages account config (complete accounts or just secrets like passwords) externally/dynamically. Backends: GitHub, HashiCorp Vault, AWS S3, JDBC, and CredHub. Services: Clouddriver (cloud provider, artifact accounts; automatic refresh supported only for Cloud Foundry and Kubernetes accounts; support added in Spinnaker 1.15), Echo (Pub/Sub; 1.16+), Igor (CI/SCM; 1.16+). Config file must be named `spinnakerconfig.yml` in `/opt/spinnaker/config/`. Vault backend config: host, port, backend, kvVersion, defaultKey, token. S3 backend: enable `awss3` profile, region and bucket; AWS Default Credential Provider Chain auth. Two management modes: complete account configuration stored in Git (`spinnaker.yml`) or Vault (JSON, e.g., `vault kv put secret/echo @echo.json`); or secrets only via Spring property placeholders (e.g., `${ci.my-jenkins.password}`). Encrypted values: enable encryption key under `encrypt` in `spinnaker-config-local.yml`. Auto-refresh: default 60 seconds with in-memory caching (configurable via `redis.poll.intervalSeconds` with Redis caching). IMPORTANT: "External configuration files (such as kubeconfig files and GCP JSON files) can only be loaded from S3 or Git (not from Vault)." (Last modified April 17, 2026) [30]

- GCP Secret Manager (official product page): secure storage for API keys, passwords, certificates; centralized management, first-class versioning, Cloud IAM least privilege, built-in audit logging via Cloud Audit Logs, encryption in transit (TLS) and at rest (AES-256), VPC Service Controls support, replication policies (choose specific regions), API-first design; integrates with HashiCorp Terraform and GitHub Actions; supports binary blobs or text strings. Pricing: $0.06 per active secret version per location per month; $0.03 per 10,000 access operations; management operations free; rotation notifications $0.05 per rotation; first six secret versions free. [31]

- GKE Secret Manager add-on (official docs): store sensitive data used by GKE clusters as secrets in Secret Manager, mounted into pods. Four steps: enable the add-on; configure application authentication; define secrets to mount via a `SecretProviderClass` YAML (supports global and regional secrets); create a CSI volume (driver `secrets-store-gke.csi.k8s.io`). Derived from the open-source Kubernetes Secrets Store CSI Driver + Google Secret Manager provider. Fully managed; no custom code; CMEK encryption, fine-grained access control, managed rotation, lifecycle management, audit logs; supported on Standard and Autopilot; Container-Optimized OS or Ubuntu node images. Limitations: no "Sync as Kubernetes Secret" feature (unlike open-source driver); no Windows Server nodes. Prerequisites: GKE 1.27.14-gke.1042001+ with Linux node image; Workload Identity Federation for GKE enabled (default on Autopilot). Auto-rotation of secrets: pushes updated secrets periodically; minimum interval 120s; GKE 1.32.2-gke.1059000+; configured via `enable-secret-manager-rotation` and `secret-manager-rotation-interval`. Auth via Workload Identity Federation through Kubernetes ServiceAccounts and IAM allow policies. (Last updated 2026-08-11) [32]

- DoiT comparison of the GKE add-on/Secrets Store CSI Driver (SSCSID) vs External Secrets Operator (ESO): ESO synchronizes secrets from cloud providers to Kubernetes native secrets (k8s secrets kept in use); SSCSID mounts external secrets directly as volumes with k8s secrets optional. ESO is CRD-based config; SSCSID requires the entire config/secret in the provider. ESO secrets work with any k8s resource natively; SSCSID needs a pod webhook and cannot easily reference secrets in ingress or dockerconfig. With ESO, if connectivity is lost, secrets already in cluster remain accessible; with SSCSID, CSI mounts can stop working on restarts. ESO is a single operator deployment; SSCSID has a privileged provider daemonset. Recommendation: if compliance requires avoiding Kubernetes native secrets, use Secrets Store CSI driver / GKE add-on; otherwise ESO is acceptable. (As of May 2024 the GKE add-on was still in preview.) [33]

- External Secrets Operator (ESO) Google Secret Manager provider: credential resolution order — static service account JSON (`auth.secretRef`), GKE Workload Identity (`auth.workloadIdentity`), GCP Workload Identity Federation (`auth.workloadIdentityFederation`), then Application Default Credentials. GKE Workload Identity supports (a) using a K8s SA directly as GCP IAM principal, (b) linking a K8s SA to a GCP SA (requires `iam.workloadIdentityUser` role and `iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account` annotation), or (c) authorizing the Core Controller Pod with no per-SecretStore config. Workload Identity Federation covers AKS/EKS/self-hosted/OpenShift via STS token exchange with IAM workload identity pools. `projectID` auto-detected from GCP metadata server on GKE; `clusterProjectID` enables cross-project. PushSecret mergePolicy (`Replace`/`Merge`, default Replace) and `managed-by: external-secrets` label for taking ownership. Replication: `replicationLocations` for multi-region; CMEK via Cloud KMS key with `roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter` and a `location` in the SecretStore. Regional secrets via `location`. `secretVersionSelectionPolicy`: `LatestOrFail` (default) vs `LatestOrFetch` (requires `secretmanager.versions.list`). [34]

- Medium (Google Cloud - Community) on consuming GCP Secret Manager secrets in GKE — 5 options: (1) Direct API fetch: "The most secure option; secrets live only in pod memory, never written to filesystem," can leverage Workload Identity for least privilege; (2) Kubernetes Secrets Store CSI Driver (native upstream driver with Google-developed GCP provider); (3) Init Container: runs a gcloud image before workload pod starts, secret stored in shared emptyDir; (4) External Secrets: upstream OSS controller syncing to Kubernetes Secret objects via CRDs; (5) Berglas: Cloud KMS-encrypted secrets stored in Cloud Storage. Explicitly not ranked by preference; teams must evaluate against their own security/operational requirements. [35]

- Northflank: Spinnaker "doesn't come with built-in secrets management." [14]
- The StackHawk integration guide stores the StackHawk API key as a Kubernetes secret (`kubectl create secret generic stackhawk-secrets`) and injects it into a Run Job (Manifest) stage; for private repos, REPO_URL "should be stored as a Kubernetes secret." [36]
- Rafay context on Vault for Kubernetes: highlights Vault features (secret storage with multiple backends, audit logs for detecting anomalies and proving compliance, dynamic secrets with TTL, encryption-as-a-service, policy-driven key rotation), and notes companies "often store (many times in plain text)... credentials in source code, configuration files, version control systems and even CI/CD tools — over time leading to secrets sprawl." (January 22, 2021) [37]

*HIPAA, SOC 2, PCI-DSS compliance*

- Stonebridge HIPAA CI/CD implementation guide (May 13, 2026): Relevant HIPAA controls: § 164.308(a)(5)(ii)(C) Log-in monitoring (attributable deployments); § 164.308(a)(8) Periodic evaluation (security scans on every change); § 164.312(b) Audit controls (recorded, queryable deployments); § 164.312(c)(1) Integrity controls (signed artifacts, verified signatures); § 164.312(e)(1) Transmission security (encrypted, mutually-authenticated deploys). Three core architectural decisions: (1) **Parent/Child Pipeline Separation** — a parent pipeline (under 40 lines) owns compliance gates, approvals, evidence aggregation, and deployment authorization; child pipelines own build/test/scan/package tasks. This prevents monolithic 1,500-line pipeline files that fail audit. (2) **Isolated Runners Per Environment** — dedicated runners per environment with scoped IAM, signed/version-pinned runner images, and HIPAA-aligned infrastructure; "shared runners with broad IAM are the most common audit finding." (3) **Security Scanners as Policy Gates** — scanners produce structured evidence (JSON/SARIF) fed into a policy engine (OPA/Rego) that blocks deployments if thresholds aren't met; scanners running as "advisory" fails audit. Reference architecture: six-stage pipeline with "evidence flowing in one direction only"; evidence written to immutable buckets (S3 Object Lock or GCS Bucket Lock) with write-once semantics; the policy gate evaluates the full evidence bundle before any deploy. GCP implementation: GCS with Bucket Lock, Cloud KMS (HSM-backed keys), GKE with environment-specific node pools, Workload Identity, Artifact Registry, VPC-SC perimeters, Identity-Aware Proxy. Tooling: Buildah/Kaniko (build), Semgrep/CodeQL (SAST), Trivy (container scanning), tfsec+Checkov (IaC), Gitleaks (secrets), Cosign (signing), OPA/Rego (policy gates). Platform preference: GitLab CI/CD + Argo CD as opinionated default; GitHub Actions workable but more constrained; Jenkins not recommended. Common mistakes: single thousand-line pipeline files, shared runners with broad IAM, advisory-only scanners, audit evidence stored in Git repos, manual approval as the only control. Conclusion: "'Audit-ready' isn't a state you achieve. It's a property of how the pipeline operates." [38]

- HIPAA Vault guide (March 6, 2025): "Encrypting data at rest and in transit is mandatory under HIPAA"; implement RBAC; choose compliant hosting providers — "Providers like Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), and Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) offer secure, cloud-native solutions specifically tailored for healthcare compliance"; use network policies and secure pod configurations; manage secrets with tools like HashiCorp Vault; automate compliance scanning with Kube-bench/Kube-hunter; continuous monitoring with Prometheus and Falco. [39]

- Kiteworks HIPAA audit-log guide (updated May 6, 2025): The HIPAA Security Rule's Audit Controls standard (45 C.F.R. § 164.312(b)) mandates Covered Entities and Business Associates implement "hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in information systems that contain or use ePHI." Required monitoring: user authentication/access events (successful and failed logins, password changes), PHI access and modification (view/create/modify/delete patient records), system-level security events (permission changes, database modifications, firewall activity, anti-malware alerts, physical access). Essential log elements: user identification, date/time timestamp, action description, object/resource accessed, access location (IP), outcome (success/failure), unique log identifier. Best practices: automate collection into a SIEM; standardize formats (Syslog, CEF, LEEF); encrypt logs at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2+); strict RBAC; integrity via WORM storage, digital signatures, or hashing; retention minimum 6 years recommended; automate alerting; align logs with incident response. Consequences of non-compliance: financial penalties $100 to $50,000 per violation, corrective action plans, reputational damage, regulatory scrutiny, legal liability, possible exclusion from federal healthcare programs. Cloud providers handling PHI must maintain detailed audit logs, implement access controls, ensure log immutability, provide log access, and sign Business Associate Agreements (BAAs). [40]

- AccountableHQ (March 5, 2026): "Strong audit trails show who accessed what, when, from where, and why — enabling detection of misuse and rapid response to incidents." Events to capture: user authentication (logins/logouts/success/failure/MFA), ePHI access (view/create/modify/delete/export/print/transmit), administrative/security changes (permission changes, role assignments, emergency "break-glass" access, privilege escalations), system/application operations (configuration updates, API calls, data transfers), account lifecycle events. Fields: accurate UTC timestamps, event type, outcome, user identifiers, patient/record context, source attributes (IP, device ID, session ID). Coverage: EHRs, clinical apps, identity providers, databases, network gear, VPNs, cloud services; standardized formats (JSON/CEF). Retention aligned to the six-year HIPAA documentation requirement with tiered storage and immutable archives. Integrity: "Tamper resistance is nonnegotiable — use append-only/write-once storage, cryptographic hashing/signing, hash chaining, encryption in transit and at rest, separation of duties, and dual authorization for purge/retention changes." Centralize with SIEM/behavior analytics to detect brute force, impossible travel, dormant account reactivation, unusual exports, privilege changes. Access controls: least privilege and RBAC, read-only investigator access, MFA everywhere, PAM for elevated sessions, redaction/tokenization of ePHI in logs, segregation of logging infrastructure. Incident response: audit trails power detection, scoping, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned. [41]

- Linford & Co. (SOC 2 vs HIPAA): "SOC 2 is a voluntary attestation engagement governed by the AICPA, applicable to service organizations storing/processing customer data. HIPAA is a mandatory federal law governed by HHS, applying to covered entities and business associates handling protected health information (PHI)." "A SOC 2 report demonstrates compliance with some, but not all, HIPAA Security Rule requirements depending on scope." SOC 2 has five Trust Services Criteria — Security, Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, Privacy — with only Security mandatory. Overlapping controls: access controls, monitoring and logging, incident response, risk management. Gaps where SOC 2 (security only) falls short: policies not HIPAA-specific for PHI access; HIPAA-specific DR requirements (emergency mode, criticality analysis) unless Availability in scope; HIPAA-specific logging of individuals/devices with PHI access; 6-year record retention. Bottom line: "SOC 2 provides a baseline for data security but does not replace HIPAA compliance." Organizations often pursue both together. (Updated 5/13/2026) [42]

*Audit logging capabilities*

- Spinnaker does not appear to ship a centralized audit-log microservice in the sources found; audit capabilities come primarily from: (a) enterprise distributions — Armory emphasizes "security controls, threat detection, and vulnerability management" and OpsMx provides "deployment observability and audit" with "audit readiness"; (b) the standard practice of aggregating Spinnaker microservice logs (see Observability below); (c) the underlying infrastructure (GCP Cloud Audit Logs for Service Accounts/Secret Manager; Cloud Logging). The Netflix SLA-metrics article documents the operational metrics each service emits (controller.invocations, okhttp.requests) which support audit/monitoring of RPC activity including "authenticated" tags. [23][27][43]

**4. Operational Complexity**

*Setup effort and required microservices*

- The canonical service set: Deck (UI), Gate (API), Echo (eventing), Orca (orchestration/pipelines), Clouddriver (cloud provider operations/caching), Rosco (image baking), Igor (CI integration), Front50 (metadata/pipeline storage), Fiat (authorization), Kayenta (canary analysis) — confirmed across the workshop transcript, Mirantis guides, and the Splunk monitoring article. Redis (cache/queue) and a SQL database (MariaDB/MySQL; SQL storage becoming mandatory) are required dependencies. [13][22][44][45]
- Bunnyshell: "Spinnaker requires Halyard, Redis, S3/GCS, a persistent store, and a dedicated ops team. Setup takes days to weeks. Many teams report 1-2 FTEs just to keep Spinnaker running." [15]
- Northflank: "Spinnaker isn't exactly lightweight... maintenance-heavy setups, limited GitOps support, and the lack of flexibility" (developers' Reddit complaints). "Spinnaker alternatives have been a hot topic lately... developers complain about Spinnaker's complexity and how much effort it takes to keep things running." [14]
- Google Cloud Community guide (Jonathan Campos): "Setting up Spinnaker is admittedly not easy. Once done I've found it to be the easiest way to automate the deployment of Kubernetes workloads." Recommended Halyard over Helm or Deployment Manager at the time. Gotcha: the default load balancer health check path is `/` but must be `/health`. Set up GCS persistent storage (service account with GCS bucket edit permissions), GCS artifact support (Helm charts and YAML), Cert-Manager for HTTPS on the ingress, GSuite login for auth, and Google Pub/Sub triggers with Cloud Build to auto-trigger pipelines. Also notes Google added a simpler installation method for Spinnaker on GCP. (2019-era post) [28]
- Mirantis quick-and-dirty guide (2018): create cluster (2 vCPU, ~13GB RAM minimum), create namespace/service accounts (spinnaker-service-account with cluster-admin), spin-gate-np (port 8084) and spin-deck-np (port 9000) LoadBalancer services; "Spinnaker has no built-in authentication, so exposing it externally is dangerous"; deploy Halyard pod, run `hal deploy apply`; pods come up over up to half an hour. [22]
- Spinnaker-for-GCP (GoogleCloudPlatform/spinnaker-for-gcp GitHub): production-ready Spinnaker on GKE, installed from GCP Marketplace; management console in Cloud Shell; Deck accessed via port forwarding or publicly with Identity-Aware Proxy (OAuth2; can take up to an hour to expose); components billed: GKE, Cloud Memorystore for Redis, Cloud Load Balancing; add admins/operators by granting Owner role in GCP IAM; add cloud provider accounts via scripts (GKE, GCE, GAE); invoke Halyard commands to upgrade Spinnaker; zonal clusters only (regional not supported); removal warning: "deletes pre-existing infrastructure as well." Repository archived on May 5, 2025 (read-only). [46]

*Maintenance burden*

- See Bunnyshell 1-2 FTEs quote above; plus the roadmap's ongoing operational migration burden (Halyard removal, SQL-migration, React migration) detailed in Section 7. [15][47]
- Splunk article: "a pipeline failure in the console may tell only part of the story due to cascading effects"; correlating logs across services "can be extremely taxing for admins"; as environments get more complicated (replica sets, additional service pods), tracing which exact pod (e.g., a specific Clouddriver pod) executed changes becomes difficult — making log aggregation urgent. [44]
- The 2026.3.0 roadmap removes/consolidates tooling: Halyard removed from the codebase (emergency fixes to 2026.2.x branch; BOM publication stops at 2027.0.0); Redis-based pipeline execution storage removed in 2027.0.0 (SQL becomes the only supported storage); Angular removed (React migration); old Kubernetes resource types removed; Titus deprecated. [47]

*Learning curve*

- StackShare: Spinnaker has "a more generic, functional interface with a steeper learning curve" vs. Armory's more intuitive UI; community-listed cons include ease of use. [16]
- Northflank notes the general developer sentiment around complexity and the "effort it takes to keep things running." [14]

*Observability integration (Prometheus, Grafana, Cloud Logging)*

- Official Spinnaker monitoring docs (last modified August 13, 2026): The recommended approach "is to attach the OpenTelemetry (OTEL) Java agent to each microservice via a Kubernetes init container, send telemetry to an OpenTelemetry Collector, and configure that collector to forward data to your preferred monitoring backend." IMPORTANT: "The Armory Observability Plugin... is no longer actively developed and should be replaced by the OTEL Java agent approach." Details: init container image `otel/autoinstrumentation-java:2.27.0`; env vars `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-javaagent:/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar`, `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4317`, `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc`, `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_MICROMETER_ENABLED=true`, `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` per deployment. Collector: `otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:latest`, ports 4317 (OTLP gRPC), 4318 (OTLP HTTP), 8888 (collector self-metrics), otlp receiver, batch and memory_limiter processors, prometheusremotewrite exporter. Backend options: Prometheus (remote-write receiver with `--web.enable-remote-write-receiver` or scrape endpoint on 8889), Datadog (API key; requires contrib image), New Relic (`https://otlp.nr-data.net:4317` with api-key header), Grafana Cloud (OTLP endpoint with Basic auth); multiple backends fan-out. Metric model: multi-dimensional tag-based; counters monotonic; "Spinnaker uses a special Timer counter type in nanoseconds emitting complementary __count and __totalTime series (divide totalTime by count for average latency)"; gauges for queue sizes/active connections. The OTEL agent auto-emits `jvm.memory.used/committed`, `jvm.gc.duration`, `jvm.thread.count`, `http.server.request.duration`, `http.client.request.duration`. Dashboards: the spinnaker-mixin project (github.com/uneeq-oss/spinnaker-mixin) provides pre-built Grafana dashboards including per-microservice, cloud provider, and "Minimal Spinnaker overview" dashboards. cdCon 2026 Spinnaker talks available via YouTube. [43]

- Netflix SLA-metrics guidance (CD Foundation, March 11, 2020): Universal RPC metrics — `controller.invocations` (PercentileTimer with tags status, statusCode, success, controller, method) and `okhttp.requests` (tags status, statusCode, success, authenticated, requestHost). Netflix alert example: Orca alert if more than 0.2 failing/unknown RPS to a specific service over 3 minutes. Service-specific: Echo `echo.triggers.count` (steady) and `echo.pubsub.messagesProcessed` (alert if subscriptions drop to zero); Orca `task.invocations.duration` (zero means Orca isn't processing new work — Spinnaker is "dead in the water"); Clouddriver `cache.drift` (cache freshness) and `executionCount` (identify failing agents; some failures acceptable); Igor `pollingMonitor.failed` (any value above 0 is bad) and `pollingMonitor.itemsOverThreshold` (circuit breaker requiring manual intervention). Netflix tracks customer-specific metrics (cache read latency, ad-hoc pipeline execution reliability). Author's critique: "No one should have to rely on a core contributor to distill information like this into a blog post!" — a documentation gap; SIG at github.com/spinnaker/governance/tree/master/sig-ops. [23]

- Splunk Observability guide: Use the Armory Observability Plugin (exposes Prometheus endpoints at /aop-prometheus on port 7002); install Splunk Distribution of the OpenTelemetry collector via Helm with custom values.yaml; `kubernetes_sd_configs` with role: pod; verify with `curl https://localhost:7002/aop-prometheus`; "Splunk Observability Cloud does not come with out-of-the-box (OOTB) dashboards for Spinnaker" — translate open-source Grafana dashboards (uneeq-oss/spinnaker-mixin) into SignalFlow; example Orca controller_invocations SignalFlow queries; troubleshooting: collector pod logs, Service Discovery ConfigMap, datapoint throttling, 36-dimension limit, metric_relabel_configs to drop metrics; Armory CD logging via direct push to Splunk HEC (default index "spinnaker"). Services to monitor with metrics: Deck (load times, error rates, user activity), Gate (error rates, request/response times, traffic), Orca (task execution times, failure rates, queue length), Clouddriver (cache times, error rates), Front50 (read/write times, data volumes), Rosco (baking times, queue lengths), Echo (delivery times, queue lengths), Fiat (authorization times, volume), Igor (job completion times, queue lengths). (August 10, 2023) [44]

- Armory monitoring best practices (Harness docs): use the Observability Plugin for environment health; metrics use a generic format (e.g., "okhttp.requests" appears in Prometheus as "okhttp_requests_seconds_count"); some metrics may be mislabeled — open a ticket with Armory Support. Application-level metrics to watch: JVM heap/GC/thread pools, queue times, cache latency. Infrastructure: CloudWatch burst budget limits and CPU, Redis/MySQL storage/IO/transactions-per-second limits, EKS, API rate limits on artifact stores. Logging: "store service logs in a log aggregator whenever possible"; the more complicated the environment, the more urgent logging becomes. [45]

**5. Pros and Cons Specific to Spinnaker**

*Pros*
1. **Mature, battle-tested deployment strategies**: Netflix provenance ("battle-tested in production by hundreds of teams over millions of deployments" — StackShare); native canary with Kayenta automated canary analysis (Waze estimates canary releases prevent ~25% of incidents); blue/green, rolling blue/green, Highlander, canary, and rolling update support; red/black deployment pattern used in production at Waze/Google; broader deployment-strategy support is considered mature relative to GitOps tools (which rely on sync). [2][4][5][12][16]
2. **Multi-cloud/multi-cluster flexibility**: not limited to Kubernetes; supports AWS, GCP, Kubernetes, Cloud Foundry, Azure (being added); "single pane of glass with visibility across your deployment for deployment status, infrastructure, security and compliance, and metrics" (Armory); designed for multi-cluster/multi-namespace workloads (Devoteam). [12][14][18]
3. **Strong authorization/RBAC via Fiat**: fine-grained READ/WRITE/EXECUTE on accounts and applications; pluggable role providers (Google Groups, GitHub Teams, LDAP, SAML groups); integration with OAuth2/SAML/LDAP/X509; service accounts for automated triggers; anti-privilege-escalation guardrails. [24][25][26][27]
4. **Enterprise support ecosystem**: Armory and OpsMx provide enterprise distributions with SLAs, 24/7 support, training, HA/DR guidance, security/compliance features (OpsMx holds SOC 2 Type 2, AICPA SOC, ISO 27001). [16][43][48][49][50]
5. **CD-only tool that pairs with CI**: integrates with Jenkins, Cloud Build, Pub/Sub, GitHub, Docker registries, GCS/S3 artifacts; good for teams wanting CI/CD separation of concerns. [14][17][28]
6. **Governance features embedded**: notifications, approvals, manual judgment stages, policy gates; supports compliance workflows (attributable deployments, approvals, audit evidence) when architected correctly. [17][38]

*Cons*
1. **Operational complexity**: setup takes days to weeks; requires Halyard/Kustomize, Redis, S3/GCS, SQL, and a dedicated ops team; "Many teams report 1-2 FTEs just to keep Spinnaker running" (Bunnyshell). Multiple microservices to operate (Clouddriver, Orca, Deck, Gate, Rosco, Igor, Echo, Front50, Fiat, Kayenta). [15][13][22]
2. **Lack of built-in secrets management**: "doesn't come with built-in secrets management" (Northflank); best practice explicitly says not to pass secrets through Spinnaker — external secret references/application-side fetching required. [14][29]
3. **Poor GitOps fit**: traditional imperative pipeline model, not declarative Git-driven; "isn't very flexible if you're trying to follow GitOps workflows" (Northflank); community votes list "No GitOps" as top con (StackShare). [14][16]
4. **CD-only scope**: requires pairing with separate CI tools; no preview environments, remote dev, or environment lifecycle management (Bunnyshell); no SaaS hosting offering (Northflank). [14][15]
5. **Declining community/momentum**: "definitely lost traction in recent years" (Northflank); "declining community" among reasons teams leave (Bunnyshell); Kayenta repo archived into monorepo (Dec 2025); Halyard removed; Spinnaker-for-GCP archived (May 2025). [3][14][15][46][47]
6. **No built-in authentication**: must integrate an IdP (OAuth2/SAML/LDAP); default installs ship with a default password that must be changed; exposing unauthenticated Spinnaker is dangerous (Mirantis). [13][22]
7. **Kubernetes rollout-strategy limitation**: cannot use Deployment objects for advanced rollout strategies with traffic management — must use ReplicaSets (CDF workshop). [13]
8. **Security gaps in edge cases**: artifacts/resources (GitHub repos, API fetches) have no permission checks (unresolved); Fiat doesn't support Pub/Sub triggers or webhook group permissions; account-scoping in config does not prevent deployments to unconfigured resources. [26][27]

**7. Current Status (as of August 2026)**

*Latest version and ecosystem developments*
- The CD Foundation published the full project roadmap on August 18, 2026, covering **Release 2026.3.0**, described as "a major version with significant breaking changes, removals, new features, and fixes":
  - **Breaking changes**: AWS V2 SDK migration (caching agents/code moved to AWS V2 SDK; "Any V1 usage via plugins or similar will no longer work"); "Angular has been removed from the Spinnaker project. For any plugins or forks, please migrate to React" (led largely by Matt Gogerly); SAML configuration moved to native Spring configuration with full migration docs.
  - **Removals/deprecations**: binaries upgraded/removed — Kustomize 5 added (Kustomize 4 updated; V3 deprecated, removed 2027.0.0), Helmfile upgraded to 1.7.0, Packer to 1.14, kubectl updated to 1.30, aws-iam-authenticator upgraded, base images upgraded from Alpine 3.20 to 3.24; native metric feeds to Stackdriver deprecated (removed in 2026.4.0); Spectator to be fully removed in 2027.0.0 (migrating to native Spring metrics/micrometer); old Kubernetes resource types removed (extensions/v1beta1, networking.k8s.io/v1beta1 — removed in K8s 1.22); **"Halyard is removed from the codebase as of this release"** — emergency fixes to 2026.2.x branch, Halyard BOMs stop publishing as of 2027.0.0; SQL becomes the only supported storage for execution data ("Redis-based storage of pipeline execution state will be removed in 2027.0.0" — Redis recommended to remain for the queue system); Titus cloud provider deprecated, removed in 2027.0.0; Front50 non-SQL (S3/GCS) storage for pipelines/templates deprecated, removed in 2027.0.0 (SQL migration instructions via Netflix migration guide).
  - **New features**: new stage to run multiple child pipelines from a single call (with dynamic arguments, dependent runs, and a required "rollbackOnFailure" pipeline — "YOU MUST create in that down stream application a pipeline named \"rollbackOnFailure\" to handle rollbacks"); Evaluate Artifacts stage (evaluates SpEL expressions inside artifact contents, producing embedded/base64 artifacts sequentially); configurable timeout on Kubernetes manifest stable checks (previously fixed 30-minute timeout); multi-pipeline runner plugin for dynamically calling several child pipelines; new Pub/Sub Cloud Account Scheduler (Alpha) using Redis streams for deterministic agent processing (replacing the non-deterministic Redis scheduler); global admin banner across all Spinnaker applications; Spin CLI API token support; UI support (admin-restricted) for adding/removing accounts.
  - **Fixes**: PostgreSQL compression failures with Orca database compression; large YAML loading failures fixed (configurable maximum YAML size applied universally); bug where newly created accounts were not read/updated across all pods. [47]
- Kayenta: repository archived December 20, 2025; now maintained in the spinnaker/spinnaker monorepo. [3]
- Spinnaker-for-GCP (GoogleCloudPlatform/spinnaker-for-gcp): archived May 5, 2025 (read-only). [46]
- The Armory Observability Plugin is no longer actively developed; the official recommendation is the OTEL Java agent (documented August 13, 2026). [43]

*CNCF / CDF status*
- **Spinnaker is NOT a CNCF project.** It is hosted by the **Continuous Delivery Foundation (CDF)**, a Linux Foundation project, alongside Jenkins, Jenkins X, and Tekton as founding projects. Netflix and Google jointly donated Spinnaker to the CDF, announced March 12, 2019, at the Open Source Leadership Summit. The CDF launched with 20+ founding members including Alauda, Alibaba, Anchore, Armory.io, Atos, Autodesk, Capital One, CircleCI, CloudBees, DeployHub, GitLab, Google, HSBC, Huawei, IBM, JFrog, Netflix, Puppet, Rancher, Red Hat, SAP, Snyk, and SumoLogic. - Jenkins was the first CDF project to graduate (August 3, 2020). [54]

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

---

## 1. Deployment Strategies: GitOps, Canary, Blue/Green, Rolling Updates

### Argo CD core GitOps capabilities

Argo CD is described by Octopus Deploy as "a declarative, GitOps-based Continuous Delivery tool for Kubernetes," and automation tools "extend its capabilities with features like configuration management, policy enforcement, monitoring, and multi-cluster management, enabling teams to enforce best practices" — "by providing integrations with other DevOps tools and better automation capabilities, these solutions reduce manual intervention, eliminate configuration drift, and enhance reliability in cloud-native environments." Many organizations use such tools "to handle complex deployment scenarios, such as orchestrating deployments across multiple clusters, automating rollbacks, and scaling resources based on workload demands." [1]

Argo CD "is a declarative, GitOps continuous delivery tool built for Kubernetes. It follows the GitOps principle that Git repositories are the 'single source of truth' for your application's desired state." Argo CD synchronizes the cluster to the state described in Git, and can perform instantaneous traffic switches and instant rollbacks via blue-green style patterns implemented with Kustomize overlays (blue-active/green-active overlays patching the production service selector). [5]

Per DevSecOps School: "Argo CD (short for Argo Continuous Delivery) is a declarative, GitOps-based continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes. It automates the deployment of desired application states to Kubernetes clusters using Git repositories as the single source of truth." It was "developed by Intuit and open-sourced in 2018 as part of the Argo Project." Architecture components include: API Server, Repository Server, Controller, Application Controller, UI, and CLI. Workflow: (1) user commits YAMLs to Git, (2) Argo CD detects changes via polling/webhooks, (3) controller fetches desired state, (4) compares live vs. desired state, (5) auto-syncs or alerts on drift, (6) integrates with RBAC, OIDC, SSO, and audit systems. "In DevSecOps, automation, transparency, and security are essential. Argo CD fits naturally because it enforces immutable infrastructure by treating Git as the source of truth." Key benefits: "Declarative GitOps, scalability across multiple clusters, fine-grained RBAC, audit logs, and real-time visualization." Limitations: "Learning curve, complex RBAC, no built-in CI, and external secret management needed." [17]

Combined with Argo Rollouts, "Argo CD is a GitOps-based Continuous Delivery tool that ensures your Kubernetes cluster state matches the configuration defined in Git. Argo Rollouts, on the other hand, extends Kubernetes Deployments with advanced deployment strategies, such as Canary, Blue-Green, and Progressive Delivery. Combining Argo CD and Argo Rollouts brings the best of both worlds, GitOps automation and intelligent deployment control. This integration not only ensures zero-downtime deployments but also adds safety, visibility, and rollback confidence to your release process." [6]

### Blue/Green with Argo CD (without Rollouts)

A detailed Blue-Green implementation guide (using Kustomize base/overlays, separate blue/green Deployments with distinct labels/image versions, individual services, and a production service whose selector is patched by overlays) demonstrates: "Blue-green deployment is an approach where two identical environments exist side by side… The magic happens when it's time to deploy: instead of updating the live environment, you simply redirect traffic from blue to green (or vice versa)." "The beauty of this approach is that the switch is instantaneous — there's no downtime during the transition. Users are seamlessly redirected from the blue to the green environment." "This is one of the key advantages of blue-green deployment — the ability to instantly roll back to the previous environment if needed." The 8-step process: installing Argo CD, accessing UI, preparing a Git repository, creating Argo CD Project and Application resources, verifying initial blue deployment, switching traffic to green by updating the Application path, verifying the switch, rolling back if needed. Includes CI/CD integration example via GitHub Actions and troubleshooting (sync failures, routing problems, pod readiness). [5]

### Argo Rollouts (official project description)

"Argo Rollouts is a Kubernetes controller and set of CRDs which provide advanced deployment capabilities such as blue-green, canary, canary analysis, experimentation, and progressive delivery features to Kubernetes." It "addresses limitations of the native Kubernetes RollingUpdate strategy," which include: "Few controls over the speed of the rollout, Inability to control traffic flow to the new version, Readiness probes are unsuitable for deeper, stress, or one-time checks, No ability to query external metrics to verify an update, Can halt the progression, but unable to automatically abort and rollback the update." Key features: Blue-Green and Canary update strategies, fine-grained traffic shifting, automated rollbacks and promotions, manual judgement, customizable metric queries, integrations with ingress controllers (NGINX, ALB), service meshes (Istio, Linkerd, SMI), and metric providers (Prometheus, Wavefront, Kayenta, Web, Kubernetes Jobs). [2]

Per Akuity's blog (March 24, 2025, Nitish Kumar): "Argo Rollouts is a Kubernetes controller and set of Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) which provides advanced deployment capabilities such as blue-green, canary, canary analysis, experimentation, and progressive delivery features to Kubernetes." "A key benefit of Argo Rollouts is its ability to perform automated analysis while rolling out a new version. With the standard Kubernetes Deployments, monitoring and responding to failures during a rollout requires manual intervention or external automation. Argo Rollouts automates this process, by continuously monitoring key metrics during the rollout, which allows the rollout to be paused or automatically rollback before the issue affects all users." "Blue-green deployments route all traffic from your current version (blue) to a new version (green) in one step — with a fast rollback path if needed." "Canary deployments shift traffic to the new version gradually, allowing you to monitor performance and stability before going fully live." Demo details: services (active and preview) point to revisions; `autoPromotionEnabled`/`autoPromotionSeconds` control promotion timing; canary steps demonstrated at 10% → 30% → 60% → 100% with pauses; e-commerce pricing engine used as example. [4]

Per Spacelift: Argo Rollouts is "a Kubernetes tool that implements advanced rollout strategies for deployments in your cluster." It "is often used in conjunction with Argo CD, the Argo project's continuous delivery (CD) tool." Workflow: 1) Deploy new app release, 2) Test the new release (developers test blue-green, real users test canary), 3) Promote to full rollout once successful — automatable using external metrics like Prometheus. Tutorial: install via Helm chart and kubectl plugin; Rollout object example specifies 10 replicas with a canary strategy "that gradually replaces pods in 20% increments, starting with a manual pause, then auto-progressing at 1-minute intervals up to 80%, requiring a final promote command to reach 100%." [7]

### Argo Rollouts FAQ (official)

- Argo Rollouts "is a standalone project. Even though it works great with Argo CD and other Argo projects, it can be used on its own for Progressive Delivery scenarios."
- Supports "BlueGreen, Canary, and Rolling Update."
- "Does not require a service mesh or ingress controller to be used."
- Integrates with Argo CD via Lua health checks that understand Rollout states (Progressing, Suspended, Degraded, Healthy).
- "Does NOT follow strategy parameters on initial deploy (creates fully scaled ReplicaSet immediately)."
- Rollbacks: "Argo Rollouts does NOT write back to Git during rollbacks; it only changes the cluster state." "No there is no endless loop… Argo Rollouts doesn't tamper with Git in any way." "Argo Rollouts rollbacks are unrelated to Argo CD rollbacks."
- "Cannot be installed centrally to manage external clusters (Rollout CRD needed in each deployment cluster)."
- Supports HA mode with leader election.
- Custom tests can be implemented via Job or Web AnalysisRuns; AnalysisRun duration controlled by metrics (interval, count, limits); "Failures = failure condition evaluates to true; Errors = controller issues with measurement (e.g., invalid URL)." [8]

### Argo Rollouts vs Flagger

From OneUptime (Feb 26, 2026): "Key architectural difference: Argo Rollouts replaces the Deployment kind with a Rollout kind. Flagger adds a Canary custom resource around existing Deployments without replacing the workload type." Argo Rollouts "uses explicit steps that you define in order. You have precise control over each phase of the rollout. Flagger uses a declarative analysis spec with automatic step progression" (increasing traffic by `stepWeight` at each `interval`). Both support blue-green: "Argo Rollouts uses a dedicated `blueGreen` strategy with active/preview services and optional pre-promotion analysis. Flagger's blue-green mode is triggered when no `stepWeight`/`maxWeight` is set."

Metrics providers: Argo Rollouts supports "Prometheus, Datadog, NewRelic, Wavefront, CloudWatch, Graphite, InfluxDB, Kayenta, Apache SkyWalking, Kubernetes Jobs, and web-based metrics." Flagger supports "Prometheus, InfluxDB, Datadog, CloudWatch, NewRelic, Graphite, Google Cloud Monitoring, Dynatrace, Keptn, and Splunk, plus custom webhooks."

Traffic management: both support Istio, Linkerd, Nginx Ingress, SMI, Apache APISIX, Traefik. Argo Rollouts additionally supports AWS ALB but not Contour or Gloo (which Flagger supports).

GitOps integration: "Argo Rollouts integrates tightly with ArgoCD (built-in health checks, actions, and UI extension). Flagger works natively with FluxCD but also with ArgoCD (with some configuration to avoid resource conflicts)." Both auto-revert to stable versions when analysis fails. Choose Argo Rollouts if: already using ArgoCD, want step-by-step control, need experiments/header-based routing, use AWS ALB/Traefik. Choose Flagger if: prefer standard K8s Deployments, use FluxCD, use Contour/Gloo, or need webhook-based testing. "Both tools are mature, production-tested, and actively maintained." [9]

From Buoyant (Scott Rigby, Jan 26, 2024): Flagger "uses a CRD that references existing K8s Deployments and creates a shadow deployment (no modification to existing workloads). Argo Rollouts replaces the standard K8s Deployment with a custom CRD (requires migration)." "Flagger's defaults cater to use cases around automated progressive delivery and rollbacks, while Argo Rollouts' defaults cater to use cases that require manual guidance through those processes." Argo Rollouts has a standalone UI and Argo CD extension; Flagger has no standalone UI but works with Linkerd's dashboard and Grafana. "Progressive delivery is a powerful technique that allows you to detect and roll back any problems with a new application version during the release process itself." Also covers: Canary Release (progressive traffic shifting by percentage with analysis/rollback), A/B Testing/Experiments (HTTP header matching or cookies/session affinity), Blue/Green (test with simulated traffic, then switch live traffic all at once; old version kept for rollback). Notes SMI is now archived; "the CNCF recommends adopting Gateway API (v1.0 GA as of October 2023)"; both Flagger and Argo Rollouts support Gateway API. [10]

### Argo CD + Argo Rollouts + Istio

From Tetrate (Jimmy Song): combines Argo CD and Argo Rollouts with Istio service mesh on Tetrate Service Express. "The development of cloud native applications has led to shift-left development with a higher iteration frequency of applications, thereby giving rise to the need for GitOps." "Istio provides richer traffic routing capabilities, enabling flexible routing and distribution based on a variety of request attributes, allowing for finer-grained traffic control and management." "Combining Istio with Argo Rollouts can fully leverage the advantages of Istio's fine-grained traffic routing." Demo stack: Kubernetes v1.24.14, Istio v1.15.7, ArgoCD v2.7.4, Argo Rollouts v1.5.1; Bookinfo app; automated canary with SkyWalking apdex metric — the canary automatically progresses when apdex exceeds 9900 (the configured threshold). [3]

### Progressive Delivery definition

"Progressive Delivery is an advanced evolution of Continuous Delivery. Instead of deploying a new version of an application to all users at once, updates are gradually rolled out to a subset of users or environments." [6]

## 2. Scalability, Multi-Cluster, ApplicationSets, App of Apps

### Native multi-cluster model (hub-and-spoke)

"ArgoCD utilizes a centralized control plane, typically residing in a dedicated management cluster, to govern multiple 'spoke' clusters across different regions or cloud providers." [29] On GKE specifically, Google's guidance: hub-and-spoke architecture with a centralized GKE control cluster hosting ArgoCD; every application cluster is added as a Secret in the ArgoCD namespace with labels (e.g., `env: "multi-cluster-controller"`, `env: "prod"`); ArgoCD's sync agent continuously watches config repositories and actuates changes across the Fleet based on cluster labels. Clusters can be added via `argocd cluster add` (inserts bearer token with clusteradmin permissions) or via Connect Gateway and Fleet Workload Identity (custom labels, Google OAuth2 token auth). [56]

Google's `fleet-argocd-plugin` (GitHub: GoogleCloudPlatform/gke-fleet-management) "automatically imports your GKE fleet cluster list into Argo CD and creates cluster secret objects for each application cluster, and keeps Argo CD in sync with fleet status changes." [59]

### Architectures compared (Octopus Deploy)

Scaling guidelines: "The general rule of thumb is fairly conservative… you should expect Argo CD HA to comfortably support without tweaks: 1,500 applications, 14,000 objects, 50 clusters, 200 devs." Performance aided by Redis caching; HA deploys minimum 3 Redis replicas across 3 nodes. Security "relies on RBAC and SSO; manifest rendering (Helm, Kustomize, JSonnet) is a potential risk area." "Blast radius" is the key failover consideration.

- **Hub and Spoke**: single Argo instance connects to many clusters. Pros: easy management, simple access, simple DR. Cons: single point of failure, lack of security isolation, Kubernetes APIs must be accessible. Best for small teams managing dev/staging/prod.
- **Standalone**: Argo instance co-located with each cluster. Pros: reliability, isolation. Cons: management complexity, complex user access. Best for edge/air-gapped, often paired with Crossplane/Terraform.
- **Split-Instance**: central management instance with components split across target clusters via tunnels. Pros: secure connections to firewalled APIs, centralized config. Cons: experimental, management complexity, limited community support.
- **Control Plane**: mix of standalone/hub-and-spoke with centralized management layer (e.g., Codefresh). Pros: centralized config, zero-trust, independent upgrades, no single point of failure. Cons: additional software to manage.

Additional: "Argo CD, or any GitOps operator should not be considered public multi-tenant user safe." "Anytime you have more than a single instance of Argo CD… there are often significant advantages to using a control plane." "Because of this we cannot recommend enough that you make sure application configurations are also stored in git." Argo CD versions have a lifespan shorter than a year (N-2 version support, quarterly releases), so a control plane "is recommended to simplify update/management overhead for multiple instances." [14]

### Architectures (Akuity, May 2025, updated July 2026, Jesse Suen)

"The 2026 Argo CD User Survey found scaling and performance are now among the most cited challenges for teams running Argo CD at scale… Scaling and performance are now the most commonly cited challenge among organizations managing more than 2,000 Applications on shared instances." "The number of respondents running one cluster per instance is declining, as organizations connect more clusters to fewer instances and feel the resulting scaling pressure."

- **Single Instance (Hub and Spoke)**: one Argo CD on a management cluster deploying to all others. Best for small teams/simple infra. Pros: single UI/API/control plane, simple install, strong ApplicationSet cluster generator integration. Tradeoffs: single point of failure; centralized credential exposure (admin credentials for all clusters in one place); scaling requires manual tuning. Recent security improvements: RBAC narrowing to specific resources, mutual TLS, automatic OIDC token refresh.
- **Per Cluster (Dedicated Instance)**: full Argo CD in every cluster, deploys only to that cluster. Best for orgs prioritizing isolation/fault containment with strict security/compliance. Pros: load distributed; no external API exposure needed; credentials scoped to single cluster; full fault isolation. Tradeoffs: configuration duplication; fragmented operator experience; ApplicationSet cluster generator unusable.
- **Hybrid (Instance Per Logical Group)**: one instance per team/region/environment group. Best for mid-sized orgs that outgrew single instance but lack platform headcount for per-cluster. Pros: load distributed across groups; blast radius contained per group; less duplication than per-cluster. Tradeoffs: still multiple instances to manage; each group needs a management cluster; group-level ApplicationSet duplicated per group.
- **Akuity Agent-Based (Enterprise Scale)**: agent runs inside each managed cluster with outbound-only access to control plane. Tested at 50,000 applications and 1,000 clusters; no external cluster access required; automatic disaster recovery; built-in audit logging. Tradeoffs: SaaS cost; less control of underlying hosting. "Reverses connection direction (agents connect outbound), removing need to expose cluster API servers or store admin credentials centrally." "No single architecture wins outright at enterprise scale; the right fit depends on available platform engineering resources and security requirements." [15]

### ApplicationSets (official docs + maintainer guidance)

Official Use-Cases doc: "An initial design focus of the ApplicationSet controller was to allow an infrastructure team's Kubernetes cluster administrators the ability to automatically create a large, diverse set of Argo CD Applications, across a significant number of clusters, and manage those Applications as a single unit."

- **Cluster add-ons**: infrastructure teams auto-deploy cluster-level add-ons (Prometheus operator, Argo Workflows controller) across hundreds/thousands of clusters. List generator = manual updates; Cluster generator = auto-detects clusters defined in Argo CD; Git generator = most flexible/powerful (JSON files or directory structures).
- **Monorepos**: manage an entire cluster's state from a single Git repo using `directories` (subdirectories with applications) or `files` (JSON metadata).
- **Self-service on multitenant clusters**: developers deploy apps without admin involvement; `template` field restricts sensitive fields (project, cluster, namespace) while allowing customization of 'safe' fields like Git source repo. "A major disadvantage is that a high degree of trust/scrutiny is needed to accept commits containing Argo CD Application spec changes. This is because there are many sensitive fields contained within the Application spec, including project, cluster, and namespace." [13]

Cluster bootstrapping docs: recommended approach is ApplicationSets with the cluster generator. After declaratively setting up a cluster with labels (cloud, region, env, type), any ApplicationSet using those labels auto-deploys respective apps. Matrix generator (git + cluster selector) example deploys apps matching label criteria (e.g., region: "eu", type: "workload"). "If you use Application Sets you also have access to all gotemplate functions as well as Sprig methods."

App of Apps (alternative): declaratively specify one Argo CD app consisting only of other apps; Helm example with typical repo layout. "App of Apps is an admin-only tool — The ability to create Applications in arbitrary Projects is an admin-level capability." Considerations: cascading deletion via finalizers; deleting child applications (consistent behavior as of v3.2); ignoring differences in child apps via diff customization; sync policy "automated with pruning enabled, so child apps are automatically created, synced, and deleted when the parent app's manifest changes"; "If you want to ensure that child-apps and all of their resources are deleted when the parent-app is deleted make sure to add the appropriate finalizer to your Application definition." [12]

Kostis Kapelonis (Octopus Deploy/Argo team) presentation: For production with many clusters/apps, "use Application Sets rather than creating individual Application CRDs." Recommended "three-layer pattern": Kubernetes manifests (Helm/Kustomize) → Application Sets → App of Apps files grouping related Application Sets. Anti-pattern "Helm Sandwich": do NOT use Helm to template Application CRDs on top of Helm for actual manifests; "if you do this essentially you will have what I call a Helm sandwich." Cluster grouping: don't treat clusters as individuals ("pet clusters"); "tag clusters with labels (environment, region, team, etc.) and use label selectors in Application Sets to deploy to groups of clusters." Use as many Application Sets as needed ("It's better to have 10 simple application sets than one monstrosity like this") — "Don't treat individual clusters. We don't care about clusters. We don't want to have pet clusters. We want to care about cluster groups." PR generator creates temporary apps for pull requests and destroys them when merged/closed. Common mistakes: "Don't confuse Application Sets with App of Apps (use both), don't use Helm sandwich pattern, don't use a single Application Set, don't model individual clusters—use cluster groups/tags." [11]

### Performance and scaling at scale (official docs)

HA overview: "Argo CD is largely stateless. All data is persisted as Kubernetes objects, which in turn is stored in Kubernetes' etcd. Redis is only used as a disposable cache and can be safely rebuilt without service disruption." HA install "will require at least three different nodes due to pod anti-affinity rule in the specs. Additionally, IPv6 only clusters are not supported." [66]

Key tuning parameters (from HA/performance docs):
- repo-server: `--parallelismlimit` (concurrent manifest generations; avoid OOM); `--repo-cache-expiration` (default 24h; 1h suggested for low-volume environments); `ARGOCD_EXEC_TIMEOUT` (default 90s; `SIGTERM` then `SIGKILL` after `ARGOCD_EXEC_FATAL_TIMEOUT`); mount a persistent volume for `/tmp`/`TMPDIR` clones; `ARGOCD_GIT_ATTEMPTS_COUNT` retries failed `git ls-remote`.
- application-controller: `--status-processors` (default 20) and `--operation-processors` (default 10); "For 1000 applications, we use 50 for `--status-processors` and 25 for `--operation-processors`"; `--hydration-processors` (default 5); polls Git every 3m by default (configurable `timeout.reconciliation` and `timeout.reconciliation.jitter`); cluster sharding increases StatefulSet replicas plus `ARGOCD_CONTROLLER_REPLICAS` env var; `--sharding-method` supports legacy, uid, round-robin, consistent-hashing (latter two experimental alpha); per-cluster `shard` field in cluster secret; `ARGOCD_APPLICATION_TREE_SHARD_SIZE` splits application tree across Redis keys.
- server: stateless; scale to 3+ replicas with `ARGOCD_API_SERVER_REPLICAS`; `ARGOCD_GRPC_MAX_SIZE_MB` (default 200MB; may need increase for 3000+ apps); `server.glob.cache.size` (default 10000).
- Monorepo scaling: "If the manifest generation requires to change a file in the local repository clone then only one concurrent manifest generation per server instance is allowed. This limitation might significantly slow down Argo CD if you have a monorepo with multiple applications (50+)." Use `argocd.argoproj.io/manifest-generate-paths` annotation (works since v2.11 without webhooks) to limit cache invalidation; fully qualified Git refs (`refs/heads/main`, `refs/tags/v1.0.0`, `refs/pull/123/head`) improve repo-server performance; `GOMEMLIMIT` to 80–90% of container memory limit mitigates OOMKill; shallow clone (`depth: "1"`) speeds cloning for large histories. [66]

OneUptime scaling guide (1,000+ apps): Step 1 — Controller sharding (3 replicas at 750–1000 apps, 4–5 larger; StatefulSet ordinal index determines shards; sharding only helps when apps target multiple clusters). Step 2 — Scale repo server to 5 replicas with parallelism limit 10 each (50 concurrent manifest generations). Step 3 — Redis HA (3 replicas, gzip), cache expiration 24h, request deduplication. Step 4 — reconciliation interval to 5 minutes with jitter, use webhooks. Step 5 — aggressively exclude noisy resources (Cilium identities, events, leases, EndpointSlices); `ignoreDifferences` for frequently changing fields. Step 6 — dedicated node pools (~27 CPU / 40Gi RAM total: controller 3×3 CPU/4Gi, repo server 5×2 CPU/3Gi, server 2×1 CPU/512Mi, Redis HA 3×2 CPU/4Gi; two to three 16 CPU/32GB nodes recommended). Step 7 — split monorepos (~50–100 apps per repo), credential templates, shallow cloning. Step 8 — alerts for uneven cluster distribution, reconciliation backlog, repo server saturation. Step 9 — disaster recovery: export all apps/projects/appsets; store in separate Git repo managed independently. "At 1,000 applications, you have crossed into large-scale ArgoCD territory. This is where the single application controller can hit its limits and cluster sharding becomes useful when those applications target multiple destination clusters." [63]

Webinar (Christian Hernandez, Akuity/Argo maintainer, Feb 26, 2025): recommends the official Helm chart (maintained by Argo community with contributions from Intuit, Akuity, Red Hat); always use `--reuse-values` before applying new values; repo server is typically first component to show trouble (especially with monorepos); sharding is cluster-scoped (not app-specific) with three algorithms: Legacy (hash-based), Round Robin (uniform but resource-intensive with frequent cluster changes), Consistent Hashing (currently alpha); clusters can be pinned to shards (e.g., separate shards per environment); recommended sync options: `createNamespace=true` and `applyOutOfSyncOnly=true`; resource annotations `prune=false`, `delete=false`, `replace=true`; ApplicationSets are "application factories" that don't replace App of Apps — both used in larger fleet deployments; dependency management via eventual consistency, App of Apps, or progressive syncs; write Lua health checks for custom CRDs; `skipDryRunOnMissingResource` for eventual consistency. [64]

OpenShift GitOps performance tuning (Thomas Jungbauer, Apr 2026): "OpenShift GitOps performance is rarely fixed by a single knob… A practical approach is to work in order of leverage: reduce unnecessary Git and render work (for example shallow clones, cache TTLs, and webhooks so you are not polling blindly), then align related timeouts (`ARGOCD_EXEC_TIMEOUT`, controller and API server deadlines to the repo server), then bound concurrency (repo-server parallelism, Git ls-remote limits, status and operation processors, kubectl parallelism) before you scale out with sharding and replicas." Recommended values: repo-server parallelism 20; `ARGOCD_GIT_LS_REMOTE_PARALLELISM_LIMIT` 20; `ARGOCD_EXEC_TIMEOUT` 180s+ for heavy charts; `ARGOCD_GIT_ATTEMPTS_COUNT` 3–5; `timeout.reconciliation` 600s–3600s with webhooks ("one of the most important performance tweaks you can apply"); status processors 50–100 at large scale; `ARGOCD_APPLICATION_CONTROLLER_KUBECTL_PARALLELISM_LIMIT` default 20, match or sit slightly below operation processors (e.g., 50); controller→repo-server timeout 120–300s. "Finally, treat tuning as evidence-led: change one major setting at a time." [67]

GitHub discussion (#6137): argocd-server workload is "mainly stateless (it keeps just a little state information in the Redis cache), so you should face no problems increasing its replicas. The same is true for argocd-repo-server workload, which can also be scaled up independently." HA manifests add high-available Redis and anti-affinity rules; upgrade requires cluster with minimum 3 nodes. Follow-up: application-controller is a statefulset; HA depends on sharding algorithm. [65]

Akuity platform scale: "The server-side pagination for the Argo CD Applications page significantly improves Argo CD API and UI scalability and allows you to manage up to 50,000 Argo CD applications!" [23]
